subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, January 23, consideration of the motion of Mrs. Shipley for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Hahn.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of this house from western Canada, I would be very remiss in my duty if I did not take the opportunity at this time to deal with the critical grain marketing situation prevailing on the prairies.
Last fall I received continued representations from the farmers in my area concerning this problem and, in addition to the representation from individual farmers, I also had the privilege of meeting with the representatives of the various farm organizations. I recall that, at the session we had with the board of directors of the Manitoba

federation of agriculture, one of the warnings they issued was that the various political parties in this house should not play politics with this critical situation. I think, Mr. Speaker, that was a very necessary warning because, almost from the earliest times of wheat production in the prairie region, there have been politicians in the wheat bin, and it has not helped at all to clarify the situation.
As I have listened to other hon. members from western Canada speak on this topic, it has been encouraging to note that there is a large degree of unanimity among the members of the opposition regardless of their party affiliations. It has been encouraging to note that it appears for the first time that we are going to have a united vote of protest on the part of the combined opposition in a matter pertaining to the welfare of our grain growing farmers on the western prairies. One of the difficulties through the years has been the variety of solutions and opinions which have been expressed by western members in regard to the grain problem. I think it will help considerably in rallying the attention of the government to this problem if we have this united vote on the matter.
If we are going to achieve any semblance of good government under our democratic system we must avoid extremes. The tendency which has been peculiar to western Canada, based largely on the continuing economic instability, to pursue extreme philosophies to their conclusion undoubtedly has worked against the general welfare of the west.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but may I ask hon. members who are supposed to be listening to try to achieve that result as much as possible.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
These differences of opinion, arising largely from the pursuit of extreme philosophies to their logical conclusions, should be worked out within the framework of national parties and not in the House of Commons on the basis of multi-parties. I emphasize again that that is one reason why I am delighted to see this unanimity of opinion at this time.
Unfortunately we have not been able to gain the support of western members who support the government, and that is quite understandable. As I have listened to the statements of the various ministers directly responsible for dealing with this matter it appears to me that there is a sharp difference of opinion in their respective appraisals of the problem. I am reminded of the opinion of Sir Winston Churchill when he was required from time to time to deal with urgent

problems facing the nation and had to consult with the economists of the day. He summed it up by saying, "Whenever I ask England's six leading economists a question I get seven answers, two from Mr. Keynes".
As I have listened to the interpretation of the problem given by the various ministers responsible I am persuaded to paraphrase Sir Winston Churchill: that whenever we listen to the answers from the various ministers, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), we get a different answer from each and two from the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
That conclusion arises largely from the speech made in this house just over a week ago by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I listened to it carefully at the time and I have since tried to analyse it carefully as it appears in Hansard. In examining it I have come to the conclusion that it was merely the use of the red herring technique, an appeal to the traditional prejudices of the prairies in order to divide the western members on this issue. It was not a very subtle appeal and not nearly so skilfully done as has happened in the past in the case of a former Liberal prime minister of this country.
The speech lumped together the Financial Post, the Winnipeg Free Press, the C.C.F. party and the farmers' union as being out to destroy the wheat board by advocating cash advances on farm stored grain. The most amazing part of the whole speech was that it linked the C.C.F. and the farmers' union with the grain exchange which has become the scapegoat for the perpetual grain problem on the prairies. That was an amazing burst of demagogical oratory and, of course, it will not go over very successfully on the prairies. There have already been press reactions to that effect.
It was further intimated that it was not the farmers who were advocating cash advances on farm stored grain but rather the city boys. As I have indicated, this is amazing to me and, having seen the situation as a western member, it is completely out of touch with reality. In fact, as I examined the speech from the throne I came to the conclusion that in dealing with this matter it was also out of touch with reality. The only reference to the problems of the grain farmers was something to the effect that some sectors of the economy are not participating fully in Canada's high level of prosperity. That is true, and it has been true over the years so far as our western agricultural economy is concerned.
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale
If we examine the history of grain production on the prairies, it has been one series of crises after another, at one time a period of shortage, at another time a period of abundance, although in recent times periods of abundance seem to occur more frequently than periods of shortage. That of course is largely due to changed production techniques, mechanization on the farms and so on. As a westerner raised on the prairies, my whole life has been influenced strongly by these continuing fluctuations and changes. My father, who homesteaded in the west in the early days, went broke during one of these critical periods.
Our problems with respect to lack of adequate financing for education, etc., largely arise from the uncertainties of the western grain producing economy. The loss of our young people through migration to eastern Canada and also south of the border in search of job opportunities is intimately connected with the unstable economic situation that has always prevailed on the prairies. It has resulted in widely fluctuating prices. It is connected of course with the inherent instability that is peculiar to agriculture and, as far as grain is concerned, arises largely from the fact that we are dependent on an uncontrollable and unpredictable export market to dispose of the major part of our production.
Today, and I would emphasize this point, the problem is much more serious than it ever was because it is connected with rapidly changing external conditions that affect the Canadian economy, among them being the declining world market for grain. In this connection it is significant to note that even India is making an attempt to become self-sufficient in the production of wheat. We need hardly refer to the stiff competition we are receiving from the United States producers. That matter has been discussed at length.
As well as the change in the external economy, we have the rapid changes in the internal economy as Canada proceeds from a primary economy depending on extractive industries to a secondary economy depending more and more on manufacturing. It only stands to reason that prairie agriculture, based largely on one product, will be caught in a vicious price squeeze as this trend continues. Surpluses are up. The costs are up. Markets are down. As a result, prices are going down. That is the essence of the situation as it faces the prairie producer at the moment.
In spite of the optimistic assurances of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and also of the Minister of Agriculture, from direct contact with producers in my own area-and we are one of the more stable and diversified

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale areas in Manitoba-I can say that there is an urgent, immediate problem today. It requires much broader treatment than the plan of government bank loans that has been referred to as the Howe plan, and the storage proposals that we shall be considering in this house within the next few days. The latter proposal will of course help, but it does not begin to get to the root of the matter which has caused this perpetual state of economic instability in the prairies since that region was first opened to settlement.
There is a short-term problem and it must be dealt with. As farmer after farmer has indicated, as have all farm organizations from the west, it can only be met by putting cash immediately into the hands of the producers. Farming has changed. It is no longer a subsistence matter where you can carry on your operation within the confines of the one-unit farm. Farming today has become a business proposition and the farmer needs ready cash, as does any other business man, if he is going to carry on his operation successfully. The only way to get that ready cash into his hands is by means of the widely advocated cash advances on farm-stored grain.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has tried to imply that the farmers are not asking for this measure and he tries to draw a red herring across the trail by saying that it is the city boys who want it and not the farmers. In my area the city boys to whom he refers are the local merchants of the small towns. In my area we have no large cities. They are the local merchants who make up the membership of our town councils, who serve on the school boards and who, in fact, carry the day to day responsibility of grassroots democracy in western Canada. They are the ones who have been making appeals to me.
Three years ago, as a matter of fact, when this surplus problem first began to appear on the prairies, we had community after community going on the strictly cash basis, refusing to extend credit to the neighbouring farm communities because the memory of the thirties was vivid in their minds. They realized that as this surplus problem continued to grow-and actually it has grown-they would not be able to carry the responsibility of financing the farm economy which today operates on a monetary basis rather than on the former subsistence basis. In fact, the farm economy is today much more vulnerable than it ever was in any former period of crisis on the prairies. Hence the city boys referred to are the town merchants-the small businessmen-who are the heart of our local government in this country of ours. Any attempt to arouse the traditional prejudice that exists


between farm and -city, between the rural areas and the urban areas, is an emotional appeal to try to stir up feelings of hostility and hatred. Today it will not take root.
Then the matter of the threat to the wheat board was emphasized. It was indicated that anybody advocating cash advances was out to destroy the wheat board. This is an appeal to fear because ever since the thirties the western farmer has clung desperately to the wheat board as the symbol for his economic salvation. When criticism of the wheat board arises, it is invariably said that at least 90 per cent of our prairie producers are in support of the wheat board. I would say that statement is broadly true. The reason the farmer is in favour of the wheat board is the instability and the insecurity to which he has been subjected down through the years. Hence you can always arouse a positive response in favour of government proposals if you imply that any other proposal is a threat to the wheat board. It is similar to the "King or chaos" appeal that was made back in 1935. Professor Lower has summed up that appeal in this manner. It will be recalled that the present administration first came to power in this country in 1935. Professor Lower describes the victory as follows:
The victory was not a tribute to Mr. King. It was not a proclamation in defence of liberty. It was not even in pronouncement on the issues of the day. Liberalism as it emerged in Canada after 1935 was the counterpart of Baldwin Conservatism in Great Britain, of Le Front Populaire in France and of Rooseveltian democracy in the United States. It represented the huddling together of frightened people uncertain of their way in a chaotic world.
I think that is a fair and honest appraisal of the situation then prevailing. Unfortunately you can still get that fear response. The farmers still cling desperately to the hope that they feel lies within the wheat board marketing of their grain which has in the past tended to iron out some of the wild price fluctuations arising from a basically unstable economy. That the cash advance formula is going to destroy the wheat board is a strange suggestion indeed, because the wheat board principle of marketing was established in 1935 in order to deal with the (repeated crises that come to our grain economy. If the wheat board cannot deal with the problem existing at the moment, anyone who makes that suggestion is merely indicating that it has fallen short of performing the task it was originally designed to perform. Perhaps it is high time that we had a complete reappraisal of the grain

marketing problem in the light of changed conditions to see wherein the present methods are impractical.
There is just one more point in the speech to which I should like to refer briefly. There was an indication that the western farmer, if he were given cash advances for his grain, might before the time period expired, dispose of the crop already covered by the cash advance other than to the wheat board. He might sell it for feed to local farmers and so forth. This implies that the western grain producer is dishonest. I feel that is the last implication that could be made in his case. I am sure the Minister of Justice (Mr. Gar-son), who comes from the west, would be only too willing to support me in this conclusion. During the thirties when governments came to the assistance of local municipal councils the farmers, at least those in Manitoba and my area, would not take full advantage of the money available to relieve them of their financial difficulties because they felt that in the long haul they would be able to take care of a major part of their accumulated indebtedness.
Farmers are essentially honest. Local governments are scrupulously honest. They do not behave in the way that the large centralized government in this country might have a tendency to behave. There is no reason at all for distrusting the integrity of the prairie farmer in this cash advance proposition.
While there is a short-term problem which must be dealt with by immediate emergency measures, there is also the continuing longterm problem which has been with us right from the beginning. As I have intimated this problem is aggravated today, Mr. Speaker, by the changing circumstances of the Canadian economy. We are moving to a secondary phase of production. Unfortunately Canada, unlike other countries that have passed through that transition, is not following the traditional paths of young countries progressing from primary activities like agriculture, forestry, mining and oil drilling into the more advanced activities such as manufacturing. We are still mainly occupied in producing raw materials which the more advanced countries like the United States make into finished products. We are hewers of wood and drawers of water for the more highly developed countries, and this has been the deliberate policy of our government.
Actually, the manufacturing share of the national income is not as impressive as it appears from a superficial observation. It has been dropping off since the peak year of 1943. We must remember that in this
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale manufacturing are included such activities as sawing logs, producing pig iron, pulp and paper, smelting and refining of non-ferrous metals. Even including those, the manufacturing share of the national income has been dropping off from the peak year of 1943.
The next point' I do not have to emphasize. It has already been adequately discussed by several members, including the leader of the C.C.F. party. This manufacturing process has come largely under the control of United States influences, and that again is a development that needs very close scrutiny by Canada. Recently, many voices have been raised on this subject. The most recent that has come to my attention has been that of our own Manitoba minister of industry and commerce, Mr. Turner. Speaking in New York last week, he invited further United States financial and technological aid in western Canadian development, but called also for a greater Canadian share in the ownership, financing and management of Canadian subsidiaries of United States companies. Canadians are not happy when they find themselves outside in their own country. These are words from our Manitoba minister of industry and commerce. This is becoming a matter of increasing interest in this country and it is something that bears very directly on the economic problem that we have in the midwestern region.
There is one more difficulty in this switch from primary to secondary industry. It is all concentrated in one part of Canada, mainly along what has become known as Canada's Ruhr valley, the St. Lawrence river. Unfortunately, because of that concentration, the western provinces are not finding the degree of secondary industrial activity to take up the economic slack that is resulting from the changing nature of our agricultural industry. I am reminded by an hon. member from the maritimes sitting behind me that it is also a problem that is peculiar to the maritimes. Western Canada is ripe for the establishment of industries. Our Manitoba minister is constantly harping on that theme. Opportunities have been missed by this government, particularly in the very extensive defence industry development.
The Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe, when he was asking for special powers to deal with defence emergencies, stated at page 5379 of Hansard for June 28, 1955:
I do not know whether they were thinking about the amounts of money I am talking about, but X can just tell you this. In the case of the Orenda engine and the CF-100 aircraft we had paid A.V. Hoe Company $122 million before the first finished aircraft was delivered.

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale
I believe $122 million would go a long way towards sparking our western Canadian economy and the production of military aircraft is largely a non-economic business. The government of Canada is the only customer and that sort of operation could take place successfully anywhere in the Canadian economy.
Private companies have begun to establish branch plants in the west. This is one of the most encouraging developments because it may overcome this long-term economic difficulty. If the government would reduce its high level of corporation taxes, I am sure we would see more of that sort of decentralization occurring. A start was made in this direction last year by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and we heartily endorse that procedure.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to bring these remarks to a conclusion, I should like to point out that Manitoba, while it is suffering from the general problems of agriculture on the prairies, is perhaps not so seriously affected as is Saskatchewan. We have a diversified economy, both on the farm and in the urban areas to a larger degree, but we are still not participating fully in the tremendous upsurge of development that has taken place in this country during the past 10 years.
Several Liberal speakers have intimated that the members of the opposition preach blue ruin. My friend and neighbour from the constituency of Lisgar made much of this sentiment that the opposition are out to preach blue ruin, and particularly the leader of the official opposition. Well, I take very decided issue with that because in his trans-Canada tour last year he preached anything but blue ruin. I have before me the newspaper report of the speech he made in Manitoba's oil town of Virden. He used words to this effect:
"Many Canadians are still not fully aware of what has happened in their country during the last twenty-five years. From the United States border to the Arctic there has been development almost beyond the scope of imagination."
Mr. Drew said he has completely sounded out the picture during his travelling throughout the country, and it boils down to a decision between developing our own country or farming out the job.
"The right answer, if we make it, will result in industrial development across the nation, increased employment and the elimination of seasonal unemployment.
"This is the beginning of Canada's golden age, an age of vast expansion and even wider contribution."
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that is far from the blue ruin charge that Liberal spokesmen have made against the opposition and against the Leader of the Opposition in this debate.


In conclusion, I say I can heartily endorse the amendment that is before the house in these words:
We respectfully represent that Your Excellency's advisers, by reason of their indifference, inertia, and lack of leadership in the face of serious national problems and their disregard of the rights of parliament, are not entitled to the confidence of this house.
There are shortages of steel, shortages of nickel, shortages of aluminum, according to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, (Mr. Howe). The United States is going ahead with a multimillion dollar steel expansion program. Russia has threatened that in the next five years she is going to outstrip the west in production. Canada has a large role to play in the west's program of development, not only internally but externally. If the government in office cannot carry the burden I would suggest that it move out and make room for somebody else who can do the job.

speechtext:
dependent on imported defence equipment. An embargo could not possibly operate fairly in such cases, and might indeed encourage armed conflict over disputed territory. I can assure you that this is no hypothetical argument.
Let us see, for instance, how such an embargo-if it could have been agreed on and enforced internationally-would have operated in the Middle East in respect of Israel and its Arab neighbours. I gather from observations made in this house and outside that this is the policy that is advocated by at least certain members of opposition parties.
This area has been one of tension and unrest and indeed danger from the very day that the State of Israel was created. That creation-it should not be forgotten-was the result of a United Nations decision which Canada supported. If the embargo principle had been adopted, Israel would have been completely powerless to defend her very existence; unless she had agreed in desperation to throw herself into the arms of communist suppliers. If it had suited their purposes, and for a price-and it would have been a high price-the Moscow government which controlled these suppliers would have been quite happy to arrange such a deal.
An alternative, which could be in hon. members' minds, would have been to permit certain quantities and types of military equipment to go to Israel during this period of tension and to allow nothing whatsoever to go to any Arab state in any circumstances. That would, of course, have been considered as an unfriendly policy by those states with which Canada has normal diplomatic relations. Neither this policy nor that of the complete embargo for both sides has, so far as I know, been adopted by any country. Indeed a policy of control which has been adopted by the United Kingdom, the United States and France, the policy which has been accepted by the free world, is that which we ourselves are now following.
Another important principle which we have followed is that of consultation and exchange of information about orders and requests- except those of no significance in quantity or nature

with certain governments who have special responsibilities in this field. We do that so that one country may know what the others are doing and thereby ensure that so far as possible the principles that I have mentioned above are adhered to.
If, for instance, we are asked to supply some ammunition for 25-pounders for a particular country-and we have been asked for that, and it is still before cabinet-we try to

find out, before taking any action, not only whether such an order would be excessive having regard to the number of guns involved, and existing stocks, but whether orders for this ammunition have also been received by other governments. The responsibility for the decision, however, is of course ours.
Now, what is the procedure by which this policy is carried out?
Under the law, as I have said, the export permit must be given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Before doing so, if the destination is one of those 34 sensitive areas where consultation is required, he consults with both the Departments of National Defence and External Affairs and acts only after agreement with those two departments. If the application is a particularly significant one, either in quantity or because of the political circumstances surrounding it, and even though the three ministers may have agreed to the permit, the matter is referred to the whole cabinet.
In the case of shipments to NATO or most commonwealth countries, the Minister of Trade and Commerce may act after consultation only with the Department of National Defence, in order to make sure that security and supply factors are considered as well as our own defence requirements.
In all cases where government surplus supplies are involved, the matter must also go to the treasury board for approval. Even after there has been ministerial agreement on an export permit, that board, a committee of the cabinet, may also ask the full cabinet to reconsider a decision taken.
Now, having indicated the procedures laid down, I should like to show how they were applied to the case of the 15 Harvard trainers approved for export last July.
In the spring of 1955 a supplier of these aircraft received inquiries from qualified representatives of the Egyptian government concerning 15 Harvard trainers. There were also received at the same time somewhat less formal inquiries about F-86 jet fighters. There was no problem regarding the jets. The reception by the government to the idea was negative and the matter was dropped even though that order, and others for jets about which we have been approached from other quarters, would have been very attractive commercially and would have assisted in maintaining work and employment in our aircraft industry.
As for the Harvards, the matter was brought to the attention of the Department of Trade and Commerce by the company and referred
The Address-Mr. Pearson by that department to the Department of National Defence and the Department of External Affairs for an opinion. The Department of National Defence studied the matter from the point of view of possible domestic requirements and of the military implications of supplying these aircraft to the particular government in question.
Information was also exchanged with certain friendly governments about the request. No objections were raised to the transaction from these or any other quarters. After all these steps had been taken, and as the matter in my judgment raised no new policy issue or important international consideration, and as the planes could not be made into effective combat aircraft, and as the request fell within the criteria I have mentioned already, I gave my approval. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was so informed and an export permit was issued in due course.

The first week in September. Before proceeding further I should like to answer the question addressed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in these terms:
Whether any field artillery weapons are being or have been dismantled and the parts sold separately by the War Assets Corporation under circumstances which would make it possible for those parts to be sold outside of Canada.
That was the question. I am informed by the corporation, on the basis of a check going back to January 1, 1952, that where any gun barrels or breech blocks have been disposed of they have been sold as scrap and in respect of each sale there is evidence available that they were mutilated prior to delivery as scrap. Such scrap also requires an export permit. Surplus field artillery or surplus artillery parts, as opposed to scrap, that is to mutilated parts, can be sold abroad but always subject to the export control procedures I have mentioned.
What are the results of this policy in respect to arms shipments to the Middle East? An impression may have been created that Canadian arms were flowing into that area in great quantities. That is not the case. The amounts involved are small and do not contravene the principles which I have outlined as governing our policy. The impression may have also been given that we were releasing modern and dangerous weapons whose capabilities could disrupt the military balance among the countries in that region and encourage all-out aggression or an arms race. That also is not the case.
There are certain figures I should like to give and I give these figures although similar figures are not given in respect to arms shipments by other countries. In 1954 export

In 1955 the figure for Israel was $1,332,110.59; for Egypt, $770,825; for all other Arab states, $70. The figures for the two years were $2,067,685.19 for Israel, and $771,121 for Egypt.
The Harvard trainers and spare parts for them were responsible for practically the whole of the Egyptian figure. The main items covered by the other figures are:
Harvard aircraft parts 75 mm. shells Anti-tank equipment
Tracks and spare parts for world war II type tanks (Shermans)
25-pounder guns and accessories [DOT]303 calibre Browning machine guns 3 [DOT] 1" anti-aircraft guns, accessories, spare parts and ammunition (This was a large proportion of the total)
The anti-aircraft guns are of course defensive weapons, and the 25-pounder guns are trailer guns in this case. In respect to the tank tracks and spare parts, which constituted a rather large proportion of the total, we were at our request given written and official assurances that they would not be re-exported and that they were all required for normal maintenance and servicing purposes for the existing stock of tanks. I have available the exact descriptions by item, quantity, value and destination of all the items covered by the totals I have mentioned. I am reluctant to make these figures public as the recipient government-there is only one in this case because in the case of Egypt the totals have already been made public-feels that, in spite of the relatively small amounts involved, the information might be prejudicial to her security. I would, however, be happy to let any hon. member who may desire, see all these details in confidence.
These figures show what has been approved. If there could be shown a similar table for the dollar value of the requests for military equipment that have not been approved the amount would be many times as great. Some requests had to be refused in toto, such as those for F-86 jet aircraft. Others covered a legitimate requirement of a type which did not contravene the principles we had established but in our opinion the amount was excessive for such requirements.
I mention these cases of rejection to make it clear that the procedures I described earlier are not merely a complicated method of in fact releasing everything we are asked for. The procedures do constitute an effective control system. This control has been applied aecause in the view of the government it is
IMr. Pearson.]

important that Canada should not contribute to the development of an arms race in the Middle East or any place else; that is, should not permit exports which would give either of the conflicting sides-if there is a conflict, a political conflict-a military advantage which the other would be bound to try to correct by increasing its military purchases in turn.
Surely the policies and controls which I have described and the nature of the exports which we have permitted make nonsense of the unfair and extravagant suggestion by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) that our actions in the field were comparable in this field with the activities of the Soviet bloc in these troubled regions. I think on the contrary the evidence is that we have been handling this matter carefully and conscientiously and with a sense of international responsibility.
I should like to turn now to the political situation in the area in order to give the background to the question we have been discussing. It is a situation which has been disturbing and unsettled, as I have already said, since the very foundation of the state of Israel. It is becoming increasingly clear that some solution must be found for the problem of the relationship between Israel and her Arab neighbours if that situation is to improve. If it does not improve it will get worse and the danger of conflict will increase. This is especially the case because there are governments which are cynically hoping to obtain political advantage from keeping the Arab-Israeli dispute burning without any concern for the damage that this would cause the Israeli and Arab people, or the danger to peace that might result. I think there would be no contribution on our part to improving the chances of peace in that area by cutting off all shipments of defence equipment to the state of Israel, if that is the policy of my hon. friends opposite.
It is the realization of this danger, the danger of conflict, which prompted western statesmen recently to offer the assistance of their governments and themselves in helping Israel and the Arab states find a solution for their disputes and problems. We in this government are very much in accord with the spirit of such pronouncements which point to the necessity of a settlement based on conciliation, understanding and compromise, which alone can afford a real basis of security and prosperity for both the Arab and Israeli peoples. The difficulties, Mr. Speaker, are great and the dangers are very real, as they always are when passions are high and feelings are deep.

We can sympathize with and understand the fear felt in Israel when they hear across their borders threats of destruction; and, of course, the United Nations did not establish _ the state of Israel in order to see its obliteration. Similarly, we can understand the feelings of Arab peoples at the alienation of land which was occupied by Arabs for centuries; we can sympathize with the sufferings of the many thousands of Arab refugees who have been made homeless. But surely to both sides the advantages of a confirmed and secure peace, instead of the present condition of precarious armistice, are so great both economically and politically that a negotiated settlement should not be impossible.
I cannot, Mr. Speaker, mention the armistice without paying tribute here, and I know the house will join me in this, to the work of Major General Burns, the chief of the United Nations truce supervision organization for Palestine. He is not, of course, serving as a Canadian but as a United Nations official. Nevertheless, since he is a Canadian,
I am sure that all hon. members are as proud as I am of his devoted and skilful work in safeguarding the armistice in most difficult and, indeed, at times dangerous circumstances, and of the high regard in which he is held by both sides for his sincerity and impartiality.
As hon. members know, I have had the privilege recently of exchanging views with Israeli and Egyptian leaders. In July the Egyptian foreign minister visited Ottawa and I had the honour of being received by the premier of Egypt, Colonel Nasser, at Cairo on my way back from southeast Asia in November. I might at this point answer a particular question put to me by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he inquired whether I would "equalize" Canada's position in the Middle East by going to Israel, in view of my visit to Egypt. I hope that it may soon be possible for me to visit Israel to see for myself the exciting and constructive things that are being done there. The reasons why I could not do so during my recent journey have been fully explained already, and I will not waste the time of the house in repeating them here, especially as they were made known to and understood in Israel at that time. I was all the more pleased, therefore, because I had not been able to visit Israel on this trip, to welcome to Ottawa at the beginning of December Mr. Sharett, the foreign minister of Israel, who came here at the invitation of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I agree wholeheartedly with the hon. member for Prince Albert that our attitude should be "equal" but I doubt whether anyone would seriously
The Address-Mr. Pearson contend that the criterion of such an attitude is an exact and prompt balancing of my journeys to foreign capitals. This "equality" which, as I say, I endorse, must rest on a sturdier basis than that.
In any event, during 1955 two cabinet ministers, two senators and six members of parliament visited Israel from Canada and each spent some time there. The members included the leaders of two parties, and, above all, they included the hon. member for Prince Albert himself. I am flattered, Mr. Speaker-indeed, I am flabbergasted-by the suggestion that all of these visits by such distinguished Canadians were more than equalled by a day and a half stopover by me in Cairo on the way home from a Colombo plan meeting.
My own discussions with Egyptian and Israeli leaders about the problems of the Middle East and my study of these problems, which I share with others in the house, have left me with the impression that, while the issues are complex and difficult, and even dangerous, there is a basic desire for peace on both sides because it is realized, it must be realized, that this is indispensable to social and economic progress. There seems, then, to be at least this foundation upon which a settlement could be reached.
I believe that the western powers are ready and anxious-I know that Canada is -to assist in the achievement of a settlement. I hope sincerely that the Soviet government and its friends are equally anxious. If they are, they will not stimulate and encourage an arms race in the Middle East which can have no good result, except for the political machinations of the stimulators. I agree, of course, with the hon. member for Winnipeg North that the way to blunt the machinations of those who seek to gain advantage from inflaming the troubles of the Middle East is to bring about peace there. I am sure any Canadian government, any government, would wish to do what it could, along with other similarly disposed governments, to assist in bringing about such a peace.
With all respect, however, I do not think that the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North made much of a contribution to that end. Among other things he complained of the "passionate admiration" of officials in the London foreign office for the Arabs. His own attitude seemed to me to be one of passionate hostility to the Arab governments. Passion on either side of this issue is not likely to help; indeed, it already has hindered and bedevilled the chances of a settlement. The hon. member implored this government to pay a "more significant part" in bringing about such a settlement.
468	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Pearson The attitude he took in the house, however, would make it more difficult, not less difficult, tor any Canadian representative, if he were charged with any responsibility in this matter, to be considered as an impartial and objective conciliator and to pay effectively what he referred to as an "honourable part".
It is easy enough to criticize indiscriminately those powers and those persons who have had to cope directly with this complex issue. It is easy enough to put forward proposals which fortunately no one is expected to put into practice. If our response to recent Soviet moves in the Middle East were to abandon friendly relations with the Arab states and support Israel, completely and exclusively, with our diplomacy and our arms, then we should indeed be playing the communist game. The moral position of the western powers in that area is based on the fact that they have, though not without mistakes and contradictions, tried to preserve peace on a basis of mutual accommodation rather than on the triumph of one side over the other. I suggest we must not abandon that position because the Russians have done so for their own purposes.
The important question is, however, how can an honourable and satisfactory solution be brought about? The main issues are now commonly known. It seems clear that both sides, if they recognize the desirability of a settlement, must give something to achieve it, must make some compromise. There can never be a negotiated settlement where one side or the other remains adamant. Each must enter into negotiations prepared for some sort of give and take although, of course, no one would expect one of the sides to make prior or unilateral concessions.
It seems to me that an essential, indeed, a first requirement, is that the Arab states should recognize the legitimate and permanent existence of the state of Israel. That, as I see it, necessitates abandonment by them of the impractical stipulation that we must return to the United Nations resolutions of 1947 which provided for a divided Palestine. The Arab states took up arms to prevent these resolutions becoming effective and I do not see how they can claim the right to have them accepted now as the price of peace in that area. The people of Israel have the right to know that their national existence is not at stake. That seems to me to be fundamental. Efforts to bring peace and all its benefits to the Middle East will be of no avail unless Israel and the people of Israel are released from the overhanging fear which naturally envelops the country as a result of the threats of destruction and of the political and economic warfare directed against it by its neighbours. Deep 

fear leads to desperate acts which, though they cannot be condoned, may at least be understood. Surely it is essential, therefore, that this basic cause of fear must be removed if there is to be a solution of the Arab-, Israeli dispute.
Just as we should like to see Israel freed from the fears and economic pressures which are being imposed on her, we must also hope that the Arab populations will be enabled to move forward toward their goals of economic betterment and social progress. There have, indeed, been concrete proofs that this is the hope of the West.
It may perhaps be said that there is fear also on the part of the Arab states lest they should be attacked. But so far as I am aware, Mr. Speaker, the 1950 tripartite declaration of the three leading western powers is still valid, that they would oppose the changing of borders by force. Moreover, the United Nations is dedicated to the prevention of aggression and the house will be aware of the fact that only recently the security council of the United Nations, in considering a most regrettable development of the Arab-Israeli dispute, gave unanimous evidence of its determined opposition to the resort to aggressive force. These, I maintain, are no inconsiderable safeguards. They would be even stronger if there were permanent frontiers settled by negotiation.
The Arab states on their part are, however, entitled to certain assurances. There must , be a fair and honourable solution to the problem of Arab refugees. That is a subject which my hon. friend touched on the other day. The unhappy plight of these refugees is of serious concern not only to the Arab countries and to Israel because it poisons their relations but also, for humanitarian and political reasons, to the whole free world. These unfortunate people have largely been maintained by the United Nations, and Canada has contributed its share toward their support. But that cannot go on much longer. Shelter and a dole are pitiful substitutes for a permanent home and opportunities for gainful work. As I see it, some compensation should be paid these refugees by Israel for loss of land and home. But it is clear that so large a number cannot return to their former land, which is now in the state of Israel whose total population is less than two million; nor in all probability would many desire to live in what would now be to them an alien country. A limited amount of repatriation might be possible such as that which would be involved, for example, in the reuniting of families. For the rest, resettlement

as an international operation, to which Israel among others would make a contribution, seems to be the only answer.
But even more important is the question of boundaries. There are at present, Mr. Speaker, armistice demarcation lines. They are therefore lines which have not been finally determined by a peace settlement. I believe that they could be susceptible to readjustments. This, of course, is by no means to suggest one-sided concessions of territory or any such thing as the "truncation" of Israel which would be crippling to the new state. But perhaps certain boundary rearrangements could be made so as to produce mutually acceptable permanent borders. There is no doubt, in my mind at least, that if the permanent borders could be agreed upon in this way the United Nations would be deeply interested in the maintenance of their security.
In return for the international guarantee which might result from this interest, with security and stability in the area which would result, I should think both the state of Israel and the Arab states would be willing at least to discuss such readjustments at a peace conference table. It seems to me also that any state which would refuse to discuss peace at such a conference table-and on some such basis of principles as that outlined above, although sketchily-would be taking on a very heavy responsibility indeed. I share, however, the optimism of the Secretary General of the United Nations, who is now visiting this area on a mission of conciliation and peace, that such an uncompromising attitude will not be adopted by anyone and that a settlement based on justice and security will be found. Please God it may be so and that this tense and torn area, the Holy Land of so many millions, may become again a land of prosperity and of peace.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reading of this statement this morning by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has served principally to expose the fumbling and floundering way in which the government has handled this issue since it arose in this house. It is not without significance that while this statement was being read by the minister ten officials of his department were reading the same statement in the gallery. I presume they have all had a part in preparing it. One naturally asks this question. With a battery of competent assistants like that why could this statement not have been prepared and submitted long ago? Indeed, since this issue first rose to the point of being a matter of discussion and interest in the house, the attitude of the government and its handling
The Address-Mr. Fleming of the issue have been characterized by evasion, want of candour, ineptitude and incompetence or a mixture of all four.
This is the 24th day of January, Mr. Speaker. It was on the 11th day of January, may I remind you-13 days ago-that this question was first raised in the house. It was at that time that the same hon. gentleman from whom we have just received this statement this morning said this as reported at page 9 of Hansard:
... I believe X can say at once that I know of no shipments of Canadian aircraft to Egypt or of any orders for such shipments.
That statement, of course, is completely at odds with the information that he has now disclosed to the house. He says he did not know at that time. However, he has told us this morning that this matter was before the cabinet at the end of the summer, that it went through various departments and that the permit was issued in the first week of September. Why the minister did not know what was going on in a matter as delicate as this, namely the shipment of arms to an area of the world that he has correctly described as one in which a sensitive situation exists, will remain a question to be answered, because it has not yet been answered.
I would ask you to look at the whole record of contradictions and evasions in the period of 13 days. If hon members opposite think that they have heard a comprehensive statement this morning, let every one of them be fair enough and honest enough to ask himself this question. If the matter is so clear, so simple and so forthright, why could it not have been delivered to the house many days ago? If it is simple, if it is comprehensive, all the more is emphasis given to the contempt that this government has shown in withholding this information from the house and in not withdrawing earlier contradictory and misleading statements.
I have pointed to that statement made just 13 days ago, Mr. Speaker. It has taken a long time to correct that one. It will not be forgotten that, on the following day when the question was renewed in the house, the inquiry was met with evasion on the part of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent).
It will not be forgotten either, sir, that the question was raised again on January 16 by my colleague the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes), when he turned to another minister, this time the silent Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney), and asked of him what shipments of military equipment were being sent over the weekend on the Star of Assuan, and the destination thereof. The Minister of National Defence
470	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Fleming made the bland reply that he had no knowledge of the matter. So far, Mr. Speaker, from the Prime Minister, from the Secretary of State for External Affairs and from the Minister of National Defence we have a sum total of no knowledge of the matter. This was five days after the issue had been raised.
Then, we move forward to the following day, January 17. Here now we are told, this time by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that approval had been given last summer for the sale and shipment of 15 reconditioned Harvard training aircraft of world war II vintage. He added that these, of course, were not combat aircraft. Then, when further discussion followed, the Secretary of State for External Affairs made this statement as recorded on page 184 of Hansard for January 17, 1956:
-I do not know how you could put a gun mounting on a Harvard training aircraft.
As he made that statement, the Minister of National Defence was sitting beside him in the very next chair but did not open his mouth. He simply turned his favourite ear to his colleague.
On the following day, January 18, now a full week after the issue had first been raised in the house, we had from the government a statement that no consideration had been given to the question of cancelling the export permit for the shipment of these training planes to Egypt. There was a statement also from the government that they knew of no reason for reconsidering the matter or believing that the permit should be cancelled.
Then again, on January 19, we have the Secretary of State for External Affairs coming forward with a limited form of correction. It was a very half-hearted form of correction of a misstatement given to this house which should have been corrected at the time it was given. It should have been corrected by his colleague the Minister of National Defence. When it was readverted to by the Secretary of State for External Affairs one would have thought that if the attitude of the minister towards parliament was a correct one, his remarks would have been attended by some form of apology for the misleading statement he had made on January 17. But, of course, ministers opposite do not apologize. They simply lay down the party line. They heed the demand of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that from now on Liberals shall toe the line whether they are in this house or in the other place.
IMr. Fleming.]

On the 19th we have this very limited form of correction by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who says on page 277 of Hansard for that date:
I am quite ready to amend and amplify the answer which I gave on this point . . .
He says:
I said X did not believe this could be done.
He was referring to the fact that gun mountings could be put on Harvard training aircraft.
Apparently it can be done.
He was well aware by that time that photographs had been issued by the Department of National Defence showing Harvard training aircraft with guns mounted on them. Is that not an amazingly generous statement from a minister of this haughty and autocratic government? He says: "Apparently it can be done." Such unwonted generosity is enough to overcome one.
Now, we move forward to January 20. Here the matter is raised in challenging form by my leader who set before the house a motion to adjourn the house for the purpose of discussing a matter of urgent public importance, namely the need for a definite government policy regarding the shipment from Canada to foreign countries of arms, military equipment and ammunition and the effective supervision thereof. Mr. Speaker, prior to the adjournment I had been discussing the government statement concerning the shipment of arms abroad. I point out that this whole issue in this house arose out of a shipment of airplanes to Egypt. It should be seen in that light and in that light alone. It is no secret that arms have been shipped abroad by Canada in recent years not simply to her NATO partners but also to countries in the very area of the globe where the troubles do now most seriously threaten. Indeed one has only to look at the publications of the Department of Trade and Commerce that are available to hon. members and to the public to see what is the value of arms shipped to Israel, to Egypt and to other countries in this troubled area in recent years. There is no surprise about that. No question was raised in regard to the shipment of arms to Israel. The Secretary of State for External Affairs this morning sought to throw out a challenge in that respect to hon. members of this house to declare whether they were advocating a complete cessation of shipment

of arms or military equipment to Israel. I wish to make it quite clear that this question does not arise and is not raised in this debate. It is rather an issue as to government incompetence and blundering and as to the rights of parliament to be treated as a parliament.
When the house heard me making some passing comments upon the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the blunders which it exposed, I am sure the house observed that I exercised restraint out of deference to my old professor. Regardless of whether or not the professors of one's student days are old in years, when one looks back on one's student days one invariably refers to one's professors of those days as old professors. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was my professor in history 33 years ago and I can only say that his knowledge of ancient history is much more accurate than his knowledge of recent history on the strength of his showing here today.
I just wished to make that comment by way of explaining the very evident restraint under which I spoke today. It was out of the deference that a former student naturally pays to his former professor; and in his charitable approach to these questions-I am speaking now for myself-he is bound to ascribe the errors into which his old professor has fallen to the fact that apparently the professor has been keeping bad political company in recent years.
In the limited time that remains I have several other matters upon which I should like to touch, although I am afraid I cannot touch on them more than briefly in view of the limitations of time. I have, first of all, a word on the subject of radio broadcasting and television.
At the end of July the government announced in this house that a royal commission was to be appointed to inquire into the whole question of the control of radio broadcasting and television in Canada. The government took another long time to announce the appointment of the commission. The announcement came about the first of December. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce were here-and we note that he has again taken his departure-we would have occasion perhaps to comment on the fact that six months seems to be the time within which the government forgets about the things it has done or promised to do.
Apparently the government nearly forgot about the appointment of the royal commission until the very end of the year, almost on the eve of the opening of the session of parliament. They finally got around to
The Address-Mr. Fleming appointing a royal commission and I have no criticism, at this stage at any rate, of the men whom they have selected for that commission; but I do wish to say that I deplore the decision of that commission not to open its hearings until the first of April. This whole question is an urgent one. The government dilly-dallied with it far too long. We were pressing for an inquiry of this kind a year ago. The Prime Minister gave some indication that he was considering it at that time but the government went on dillydallying in a manner that is so familiar to this house, and now this commission has announced that it is not going to commence its hearings prior to the first of April.
I regret that very much because it means, of course, that debate on the subject is going to be hampered during the course of this session and it is quite evident that we cannot expect the report of the royal commission to be available at the present session. If the government is contemplating an election this year this would neatly serve its purposes. I do not suggest that the commission has deliberately been a party to meeting the government's exigencies in this matter, but it is unfortunate that the delay in the opening of the sittings is going to create that benefit for the government in trying to cover up the short-comings of its policies in that respect and this tremendous burden of cost under which virtually the whole policy In regard to television is breaking down today.
I have time to make only one comment on the matter of political telecasting. It is evident from the speech the Prime Minister made in this house two weeks ago that he personally has had a good deal to do with delaying political telecasting in this country. It suits the interests of the government to keep political telecasting from the people because, of course, government ministers are frequently called upon to broadcast over television. When we raised this question in the radio committee last spring we were told, of course, that when these ministers are telecasting they are making statements of general interest to the country, as though no member of the opposition was ever to be called upon to make comments before a television audience on similar matters.
The reason the government has been delaying any sensible attempt to make political telecasting available to the Canadian people is quite evident; they have the advantage now, they are exploiting that advantage, they want to continue to claim that advantage, and to play the dog in the manger. This cannot be held up any longer. It is about time the government grew up in this respect and realized that other countries have political telecasting. There is no

The Address-Mr. Fleming reason why Canada cannot have it on the basis of a fair division of time among political parties. Moreover, we do not propose to submit to any form of government censorship in that respect, as was proposed by the representative of the Liberal .party who attended the recent meeting of political parties with officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to discuss this subject.
I have just one comment to make on one matter that was raised by the hon. member who moved the address. It is in regard to the appointment of a woman to the civil service commission. For my part I support and advocate the appointment of a woman to fill the present vacancy on the civil service commission, as I think I was the first member in this house to advocate some years ago the appointment of a woman to the board of directors of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I should like to say now I entirely support the proposal to appoint a woman to that commission. There are capable and competent women available for the appointment.
I have just one or two observations to make to the Minister of Finance. I realize that perhaps by the time this subject is next discussed his proposals may already have been introduced to the house, but in framing his budget proposals I hope he will not overlook three things that have been overlooked in the past and which are now crying for immediate remedy. The first is that the limitation upon the policy and the legislation of making grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes, where the federally-owned property exceeds 2 per cent of the total assessment roll of the municipality, ought to be widened. Those provisions should be widened so that grants will be made to municipalities out of the federal treasury equivalent to taxes on all federally-owned property in municipalities. These municipalities are suffering today very greatly from an urgent need of revenue. They are obliged to provide services for these properties and the provision of such services is not confined to municipalities where the federally-owned property happens to exceed 2 per cent of the total assessment roll.
The second point is that the federal sales and excise taxes on goods purchased by municipal bodies, whether municipal councils or school boards or boards of education, should be eliminated. We have advocated this for years, and the time has come for action.
The third point to which I hope the Minister of Finance will give effect in writing his budget proposals is that the present exemptions from income tax, $1,000 for single persons and $2,000 for married persons, are entirely inadequate and should be increased.


If the Minister of Finance is not prepared to go as far as Conservative policy advocates in this respect, namely $1,500 for single persons and $3,000 for married persons without dependents, then at least we hope he will take a generous step in that direction.
There is one other matter quite unrelated to what I have been discussing with which I should like to deal. In view of recent events I think it should be commented upon. I refer to the succession of crimes committed upon young girls in a number of Canadian cities. This has been mentioned by several hon. members previously in this debate. The expression "sex deviate" is I think too euphonious to apply to the kind of people we are speaking of. I do not share in the inclination to speak of these people as though they were just sick, as though they were well-meaning people who could not be held to be responsible for the results of their criminal acts. I think we will be taking a more realistic approach to this problem, for problem it is, if we call these people by their true names, criminals, rapists, murderers, brutal inhuman monsters.
In London, Hamilton, Toronto and other cities there has of late been a shocking succession of crimes of this kind. The public is aroused today as it rarely has been. It is a great pity that the report of the royal commission which is studying this question or some aspects of it is not now available. Let us hope that it will be available early enough during the course of this session so that whatever legislation may be intended to arise out of that report may be brought into effect at this session.
Part of the trouble of course is inadequate enforcement of existing laws and inadequate police forces to cope with crimes of this kind which are usually practised by stealth. I think the unhappy and sordid experience has pointed to the need of strengthening the law in relation to the protection of society. That points in the direction of detention. When I speak of detention I do not mean just to pat these criminals on the head and tell them to be good boys. The warning I should like to give is a warning against a soft approach in dealing with this problem. We are not dealing with soft people, we are dealing with monsters and murderers.
I had wished to say something today concerning our trade but I fear that that must wait for another occasion.
I wish to close these remarks by directing some observations to hon. gentlemen opposite who in the last analysis by their attitudes at this session will determine whether there is or is not to be a change in attitude on the part of the government. Let me say to them that the attitude of the government toward

parliament which was manifested last summer in the debate on the defence production bill is evident again. There is no indication as yet that this government has learned the sound and salutary lesson which it ought to have learned from that experience of last summer. Apparently we are just back where we were before with the government determined to have its own imperious way regardless of parliament. We, Her Majesty's loyal opposition, must continue to fight for parliament's rights and to defend those freedoms of the people which are inherent in parliament and in a proper relationship between parliament and the government. Make no mistake about it, if that battle has to be waged we are here to wage it. But it rests with hon. gentlemen opposite, the private members supporting this government, to decide whether there is going to be a continuance of that haughty and overbearing attitude toward parliament.
There have been certain developments in this house since the conclusion of that historic and momentous debate last July. At that time there happened to be at least two Liberal members of this house who were independent in their approach and who over the years stood firmly on their feet and even on occasion did not hesitate to be critical of a course of action taken by the government. But those two hon. members are no longer with us. I refer to the former member for Spadina and the former member for Temiscouata. Whatever there was in the Liberal ranks by way of independence as represented by the attitude of those two hon. members has now been removed from the Liberal membership in this house.
We do not hear an independent voice of any Liberal in this house any more. The member for Spadina, to whom I referred, has been succeeded by a Conservative member, and properly so. The former member for Temiscouata, with his original and independent approach to questions, has been succeeded by an hon. gentleman who while vocal enough during his campaign has since proclaimed that he will be mute in this session and has imposed upon himself a self-denying ordinance of vocal asceticism.
I can only say to that hon. gentleman at the outset of his parliamentary career, and I do so in good part, that he should carry on the tradition of Temiscouata, the tradition of independence, the tradition of a member who stands up and does not forbear to be critical of the government and its errors. An example
The Address-Mr. Bertrand has been left by the hon. gentleman who preceded the hon. member and who made the name of that riding famous in this house and throughout the country. He did not make that name famous by being a mere sycophant of the government, and I commend his example to his successor.
In the amendment introduced toy my leader we have complained of a lack of leadership on the part of the government, of its indifference and its inertia. We see in this government a complete unwillingness to face up to problems. The problems are there and every member of the house but the government knows of them. Hon, members from the prairies representing the government, like the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) for instance, know what kind of a wheat problem there is today and how it jeopardizes the whole economy, not only that of the west but of all Canada.
We wish to hear these voices of Liberals from western Canada. We have heard very few of them so far. They are voices that ought to be heard, and in the absence of leadership on the part of the government I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is about time for some of the backbenchers opposite to be heard to draw to the attention of the government the existence of these problems. The government has no solution. The government has ceased to think, but the denial of solutions will not cure the problems. The problems are there. We demand action.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be long in my remarks but I thought I had to call the attention of the government during this debate to a situation existing in my county and which concerns more particularly the rubberized fabric footwear industry. I believe that it is here in the house that members of parliament should, with as much sincerity in their words as loyalty towards their constituents, voice the representations which have been made to them and deserve to be brought to the attention of those who run the country.
In these last 16 years I have never been reluctant to speak in this house on behalf of the people of Terrebonne county who, four times, have shown me not only their usual unflagging friendship but also increasing confidence. I have never been reluctant either to speak in this house for any group that might think itself aggrieved by the laws of this country and, with a courtesy I want to mention here, would come to me with its representations.
