The Address-Mr. Bertrand
At this time it is the officers of the Dominion Rubber Company, in St. Jerome, the employees of that plant and the labour organizations of that city who request my support in order that the Canadian rubberized fabric footwear industry be not jeopardized any further by the importation of the same kind of footwear made in Hong Kong, and particularly in Japan, and which are being dumped in large quantities on our Canadian market.
I believe there are in Canada seven companies directly concerned with the manufacture of rubberized fabric footwear. They are B. F. Goodrich Canada Limited, in Kitchener, Ontario; British Rubber Co. Limited, in Lachine; Acton Rubber Limited, at Acton Vale; Kaufman Rubber Co., in Kitchener; Miner Rubber Company Limited, in Granby; United Rubber Limited, in Toronto and Dominion Rubber Co. Limited, in Montreal. This last named company operates a very large plant in St. Jerome, in the county I represent.
These companies, I take it, manufacture leather footwear, tires and other products, but all manufacture canvas footwear and rubber footwear, rubber being a basic product they have to use in various ways. However, I understand that the manufacture of canvas and rubberized fabric footwear, becomes, though in varying degree, an indispensable factor in their general progress.
I know that in my constituency, at St. Jerome, there is an extensive production of rubber soled canvas footwear and of waterproof rubberized footwear, including overshoes.
I am told that, in the field of rubberized fabric footwear, the Canadian production which, in 1947, was 24 million pairs, had gone down to 12 million pairs in 1954. I am also told that whereas the pre-war export figure of rubberized fabric footwear was six million pairs, the corresponding figure in 1954 was only 92,000 pairs, including a high proportion of special types.
It is not my intention to enter into a lengthy enumeration of figures and statistics; the government knows about them. But I do wish to dwell for a moment on the reasons for this state of affairs. Canadian production of canvas and rubberized fabric footwear has decreased significantly. Production for export, in fact, has gone down so much that, right now, it is practically non-existent. The explanation, it would seem, is that our Canadian products must face the unbearable competi-

tion of similar products manufactured in India, the United Kingdom and mainly Hong Kong, products which have access to our markets, under trade treaties. This situation will become even more desperate since Japan, which now has a trade treaty with this country, is also flooding our markets with canvas and rubberized fabric footwear, Japan has always been and is still recognized as a major producer of that commodity.
A few years ago our Canadian firms could serve the domestic market and also produce millions of pairs for export. Now not only have they lost their export market but they are also in the process of losing their domestic market too. Imports into this country of canvas and rubberized fabric footwear are constantly on the increase. These products, which are manufactured by extremely cheap labour can be sold in this country, with all taxes paid, at a price far below the very lowest manufacturing costs of the same product in Canada. Here are some figures which have been provided by the federal bureau of statistics. In October 1955, 211,903 pairs of canvas footwear entered the Canadian market as against 4,568 pairs in 1954. In October 1955, 163,593 pairs of waterproof rubberized fabric footwear entered this country, as against 89,981 in 1954.
I gather from these few figures that the rubberized footwear industry in Canada is at a low ebb. On June 22 last, their representatives officially presented the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) with a brief during an interview at which I had the privilege to be present. Later on, a committee consisting of the representatives of the departments, companies and trade unions concerned, was set up to review the situation. And all I could personally find out is that the Dominion Rubber plant, at St. Jerome, is no longer operating at capacity, the number of workers that used to be employed in that plant has been substantially reduced, and that the people are deeply concerned about it.
The Canadian rubberized fabric footwear industry has requested an embargo on those products. My information is that the government could not grant this request for the only reason that Canada, having signed treaties with the countries referred to, has to take the products that those countries manufacture if it wants to sell them products that they lack. Now, in those countries I am referring to, the manufacture of canvas or rubberized fabric footwear represents a prosperous industry,

and Canada seems to be forced to take their products, even though by so doing it prejudices and paralyzes production in the Canadian industries concerned with the manufacture of similar products. That, I believe, is the reply given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris). In his opinion, he must first consider the general economy of the country and Canada must keep its rank in international trade. I know that if we trade with someone the advantages cannot all be on the same side and that concessions, which sometimes hurt, must be made. If I am not mistaken, the volume of goods we sell to these countries greatly exceeds that of the goods we buy from them. That deserves consideration, which proves, Mr. Speaker, that it is not always easy to govern a country like Canada.
It remains, however, that Canadian industries are seriously prejudiced in their production by the treaties we sign. Let us suppose for a moment that the government, for the most legitimate reasons under the circumstances, could not prohibit the importation of foreign goods into Canada. Could it not, however, by revising its trade treaties, set a maximum quantity on canvas rubberized fabric footwear admitted into Canada? At present, our companies are faced with the constant threat of imports increasing even more from month to month and they are appalled at the prospect of an industry going to ruin, an industry built up at the cost of great sacrifices and on which so many other fields of economic activity are dependent.
If the government did set a quota on the volume of canvas or rubberized fabric footwear that foreign countries could ship to us, Canadian companies could at least know the eventual extent of the competition and then take steps to face it, either by means of publicity, or by new methods of production, or by manufacturing new and more attractive types. At present they are loathe to adopt a definite stand. They simply see the fruit of long years of labour crumbling before a situation they have to accept, that is forced upon them. Under the circumstances, it is impossible for them to face competition. Shoes from Hong Kong and Japan, which are of good quality, I am told, are sold, however, at much lower prices, for the simple reason that salaries paid in industries in Hong Kong and Japan are ridiculously low. I am assured that the salary of a woman represents 6
The Address-Mr. Bertrand cents an hour and that the man earning 15 cents an hour must have an exceptional yield. At the same time, it is quite obvious, the average salary paid in our footwear industries amounts to $1.45 an hour. There is also a matter of employment. I understand that at present employment in this country reaches an unprecedented high but, nonetheless, some cities must not be deprived of their share of national prosperity. In St. Jerome, several hundred workers, employed for years by the Dominion Rubber Company, do not work at their regular jobs because the factory no longer manufactures for export and is slowed down to the level of the local market which is already saturated with imported products.
In my opinion, the government could do something. It is not so much the case of the Dominion Rubber Company that I am pleading at this time as that of the working class of my constituency. I am not much of an economist, but I dare say that, if the government has to stick to its decision and, first and foremost, consider the economy of this country as a whole; if, in order to ensure a still more marked advance in other and perhaps more elaborate fields of our national economy, the government necessarily has to jeopardize existing Canadian industries, it should also, to my mind, adopt certain legislation to compensate the losses sustained by these industries because of government decisions.
We are paying subsidies for wheat; I am not opposed to this, for it is an important phase of our economic life. We are devoting large sums of money to the support of agricultural products; I don't object, for agriculture is the wealth of a nation. I am aware that it is not a matter of compensating the losses of private companies by means of a subsidy, but I wonder whether the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) could not, in all cases where Canadian industries are in any way prejudiced because of our laws, give them a priority with regard to the numerous contracts his department is placing every year, and which, I think, these industries could easily accept without much retooling. It seems to me that this would be only fair. What I am primarily aiming at is to have in my county, as well as everywhere else, an abundance of remunerative employment. established principle that Canada is a bilingual country. May their example inspire all Canadians, particularly those who are at the head of the various departments of the federal administration. Unfortunately, many of them seem to ignore completely the principle of bilingualism.
I should also like to avail myself of this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to salute the electors of the constituency of Quebec West whom I have the honour of representing in this house and to assure them once again of my most faithful devotion. May I be permitted to say to my electors, and more particularly to those of the labour classes who form the great majority, that for them I shall not cease to ask all they need not only to ensure their existence but to make them feel that they are on the same level with the other classes of society. This leads me to ask the government to give special attention to the alarming unemployment problem which still prevails this winter in my constituency and also in the whole city of Quebec. Even though the federal statistics proclaim an improvement in the employment situation, the fact remains that the situation is just as serious this winter as it was last year. The statistics published are far from representative of the true situation. They merely indicate the number of those who receive unemployment insurance benefits and forget to mention those who, by the nature of their work, are not eligible to receive such benefits but who are unemployed nevertheless.
Furthermore, there are those who do not possess a sufficient number of stamps to entitle them to collect any benefits. What of those who have already used up all the benefits to which they were entitled and no longer receive any? They are not included in these statistics. Last but not least, we find a great number of unemployed persons whose rightful demands have been rejected because of this interpretation of the law by an allpowerful bureaucracy. It is only by adding up all these unemployed persons that a true picture of the unemployment situation is given. This is something the government is not interested in making public in order to conceal its own incompetency in finding a solution to the problem. I shall return to this subject in a few moments.
Until the situation improves, would it not be possible to undertake more public works as they are the only truly efficient remedy?

I have often requested public works of a nature that might be helpful to the unemployed, works which would improve the lot of the working people and would also provide improvement in the field of public health to the benefit of my fellow citizens. The St. Charles and Lairet rivers which cross my city did not improve during the past year and continue to threaten public health. These two open dumps, which are a local and national disgrace, still continue during the summer months to spread foul and dangerous odours over the city of Quebec. Incidentally the extremely hot summer we had last year contributed to imposing upon our people a torture that they alone can describe.
When will the government decide to take some action? When will the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), as the member for Quebec East, give some thought to his poor electors who are considered as real orphans without any representation in the parliament of Canada? I ask the government and more particularly the Prime Minister to have, if not affection for those he is supposed to represent, at least a little sympathy. The people of Quebec pay their taxes to their government and I believe they are entitled to a little more consideration. I repeat what I stated in Quebec on October 25 last when reporting on my mandate. I have no objection to protecting the health and life of those who live thousands and thousands of miles from our country. However, if the government refuses to apply to the letter the proverb that charity begins at home, then I think it is only logical we should demand that they should begin protecting the health and life of those who daily contribute their work, their labour and their taxes to the greatness and prosperity of Canada.
If instead of spending the summer at St. Patrice de Riviere-du-Loup, 120 miles from Quebec city, which is situated on the enchanting shores of the river that bears his name, the Prime Minister had decided to build a summer home on the shores of the Lairet river, he would have soon freed his constituency from the foul smell which, like his electors and mine, he would have been compelled to breathe. The Prime Minister behaves, therefore, perhaps not with wisdom but at least with caution by staying 120 miles from his constituency during the summer, since this is the best way to remain in good health.
As for the electors of Quebec East, those poor orphans who never see their member except in the newspapers, they are far less important. They continue to be poisoned little by little through contact with these rivers. Nevertheless they have the satisfaction, if I may call it that, of saying that they

I would venture a suggestion to the Prime Minister in this connection. If his government does not want to undertake this work, if it prefers to throw federal responsibilities on the shoulders of the provincial government, why does it not grant the city of Quebec an annual subsidy which would allow the municipality to undertake the work? This subsidy would be a logical compensation for property taxes the government does not pay on its many buildings and sites. If this were done, the federal government would be following the generous example set by the government of my province which has granted the city of Quebec a subsidy of $1 million to help solve its administrative problems. Just two years ago the provincial government granted a quarter of a million dollars for the same purpose. If the Prime Minister could accept that suggestion, which would be beneficial to Quebec, and would specify as the purpose of the grant the deepening of the St. Charles river and the reclamation of the Lairet river, I would be the first to congratulate him in the name of those who, for too many years, have had to put up with these dumps.
Another means of helping the working class and of fulfilling in some way the needs of these larger families would be to increase family allowances, even doubling them if possible, because the cost of living has more than doubled since the enactment of that social legislation. There is not a single government, not a single industry, that has not substantially increased the salaries of its employees since 1945. Even the indemnity of the representatives of the people has been doubled under the pretext that the cost of living has risen in that proportion. How could one argue today, Mr. Speaker, that family allowances fulfil the aims for which they were established when one knows that the 1945 dollar has lost more than 50 per cent of its value? I urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) to discuss this important matter with his colleagues in the cabinet and bring forth the necessary remedy at this session.
While I am on the subject of social security, may I be permitted to ask the minister to amend, with the least possible delay and make more generous the legislation enacted at the last session to help disabled people. It should extend to all those who, at birth or later in life, are affected by a disability or disease which prevents them from earning their living. As it stands, the act helps only a few and I am under the impression that the cost of administration is as high as the cost of the pensions.

The Address-Mr. Dufresne
I wish to thank the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) for having agreed, after numerous protests it is true, to postpone the implementation of the rule which prevented stevedores and seamen who operate on the St. Lawrence and the great lakes from drawing their unemployment benefits during the winter. This rule was the work of bureaucracy and a blatant injustice to these seasonal workers. If these people cannot engage in their regular occupation during the winter, it is not through an act of chance but through an act of God. If they did not get these benefits to which their numerous contributions entitled them, I can tell the minister that the economic expansion of my city and my district would be seriously prejudiced.
Speaking of bureaucracy I should like to tell this same minister, if he does not know already, that the employees of the various unemployment insurance commission offices have a handbook that was drafted and distributed by the senior officials of the commission and which deals with the interpretation of the act passed by parliament at the last session. If I recall correctly, under the legislation enacted last year the amount of benefits was increased while the number of weeks during which an insured worker drew benefits was decreased. I want to tell the house that since the enactment of the new legislation the commission has paid much less than before. Through the intervention of bureaucracy and its interpretation of the act, I assert that at least 60 per cent of the claims submitted to the Quebec offices are rejected.
Thus, distress and difficulties are on the increase in our families. This, Mr. Speaker, through the complacency of the government in power, is still another encroachment of bureaucracy upon the supremacy of parliament. Legislation must be applied according to the spirit of the lawmaker and not sabotaged through the whims and fancies of bureaucrats whose influence is growing ever more dangerous to the prosperity of this country. I am not blaming in the least the minor officials, but I do blame those who in certain departments and commissions seem to have more authority than the minister himself and parliament. It is more than ever time to put a brake on the influence of a few overly ambitious bureaucrats and to return to the true democratic system; that is to the authority of the people's representatives responsible to those same people.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on something which was the subject matter of a question I put a week ago to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), concerning the sale of butter to communist countries.
{Mr. Dufresne.]
Nobody in this house was opposed to the establishment of a support price for butter of 58 cents a pound. On the contrary, every member supported this measure on the ground that it safeguarded the dairy industry of this country. This industry is so important that it would be unwise to prejudice it in any way.
However, because of the inertia of the government and its excessive optimism, and because also of the incompetence and lack of foresight of those whose business it was to conserve our markets, we find ourselves in a deplorable position. We have had to keep in storage, regularly over the years, approximately 60 million pounds of butter, and this year over 80 million pounds.
The consumer must still pay between 63 and 65 cents a pound for this commodity, besides having to pay, through his taxes, the difference between the support price and the selling price; that is, about 25 cents a pound.
Production being far above domestic consumption, the government decided to sell its surpluses in the communist countries. If every pound of butter sold in those countries had corresponded to the price paid by the Canadian consumer, or, at least, to the price guaranteed the producer by the government, there would have been no protests such as those which have arisen in all parts of this country. But when one thinks that Canada is selling butter to communist countries at 37 cents a pound while the Canadian consumer pays at least 25 cents per pound more for the very same butter, I say that that is a policy of exploitation of public funds for the benefit of the most dangerous enemies of democracy. While Moscow continues to sell its satellites, at a good price, deadly weapons which might eventually be turned against us, the Canadian government is exploiting the labour of our farmers and the taxes of our fellow citizens by selling butter at bargain rates. That is going beyond the bounds of generosity. It is such as to bring upon us economic chaos and ruin.
Why should the Canadian people not benefit from this generosity? They are the ones who are constantly paying the shot. Why, for once, should they not at least have the satisfaction of paying for something for themselves?
I, therefore, object with all my energy to the money and work of the Canadian people being used to feed our most dangerous enemies, those who nurse the hope of crushing us in order to establish in Canada the policy of slavery and persecution so much in honour in these countries under the whip of the

Kremlin. If we do not put a stop to government extravagance, it will not be surprising to see before too long our surpluses of butter being shipped to red China, which the government is about to recognize.
A debate is to be held shortly on the recognition of communist China, a debate in which I will certainly take part, so I shall not deal any further with this matter today. Suffice it to say that this recognition by Canada would amount on our part to giving our agreement to slavery and our guilty approval to concentration camps and religious persecution. In a word, it would amount to voting in favour of banditry in its most heinous form.
Mr. Speaker, how can you expect the Canadian people not to look forward to an opportunity to pronounce its verdict on its administrators and by this verdict condemn their policies which are becoming increasingly disastrous for the future and security of Canada?
The Liberal party is panic-stricken in the face of failure of its administration and the fate it can expect at the next general election. They can amuse themselves on the other side of the house and take the situation lightly, but we feel more than ever before the indignation of a whole population, and in-digation which will manifest itself soon by the fall of the regime.
The Conservative party, to which I have the honour to belong, led by a man of vision and a great statesman, is making giant strides on the road to victory which will mean the liberation of the Canadian people from a party that was once great because of its leaders, but which is now being drawn rapidly into the valley of humiliation. Already we have significant signs of the defeat in store for that party. The last by-elections in the country have shown clearly that deliverance is not far away.
Confusion and discord are rife in the Liberal party, and the younger members would like the old guard to disappear, particularly those who have been in the cabinet twenty years and have come to look upon themselves as the dictators of this country.

After listening to a portion of .the debate this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I wonder just what the purpose of our meeting in parliament really is. I believe that once again we have come together in a parliamentary session for intelligently reasoning together and exchanging counsel on all those things which affect our people and the conditions in which they presently live. We are here to re-examine methods in order that we may operate successfully in the future and keep our communities and our country strong. In that respect I believe every single member has an important role to play and at the very outset of the session I believe it is a good idea for us to evaluate that role.
This parliament accepts as the symbol of progress the right of members to justly criticize and give full and unrestricted expression to their thoughts. This, of course, does not preclude members on the government side from continuing to backslap their government

for past accomplishments and repeating unimportant platitudes with respect to their present policy. I do not wish to offend anyone, but it seems to me that is not characteristic of a progressive democracy. The decisive characteristic of a progressive democracy is the far more important right and, indeed, the duty of members from all parties to offer a better way, better ideas and better alternatives to many of our present policies which today deny making economic and social security, with freedom, abundantly available to all our people.
We believe that the strengthening of our way of life can best be done by constructive criticisms and the early acceptance and management of our affairs on solid moral and economic principles. We are dedicated to such a cause, and we in the Social Credit movement shall continue to call upon the people of Canada to recognize that this movement is indeed the alternative to the old line parties. Our parliament meets at a time when there are certain happenings in the world which stress the urgency of putting our own house in the very best order. There are many opportunities for us to do that. The speech from the throne contains the following:
* Canada has enjoyed, on the whole, a high level of prosperity. Some sectors of the economy have not fully participated in this increased well-being.
I repeat:
Some sectors of the economy have not fully participated in this increased well-being.
May I just dwell on that for a moment. We live in one of the wealthiest countries in the world. I certainly do not know of any other place on God's earth that has the potentialities for development which face us here in Canada in abundance. We have enormous quantities of the best wheat in the world; food, clothing and all the other essential materials from our fields and our factories. Great as our production is, it is only a scratch on the surface compared with what it could be if we gave inducements for capacity production. When we add to this picture the political freedom of our society, then surely we recognize that this parliament has the greatest opportunities ever, not only to raise the living standards of Canadians to the very highest levels but also to help others raise theirs.
By doing this we will not only be serving humanity but also making a contribution toward reversing the present setback which the free world has experienced in international affairs. Let us be honest. The struggle between the east and the west is not going well for our side. Since in my opinion communism is simply the outgrowth and essentially the result of people losing 67509-32
The Address-Mr. Holowach faith in there being another way to resolve injustice, exploitation and hunger, there is a big job to be done. This job is to make democracy so dramatically dynamic and real that all will want to emulate us.
In order to make that a reality I believe we should come to grips with the essential issues. Clearly the problem is not one of production. The grain growers of our west have produced record crops, but their sector of the economy has not fully participated in the increased well-being. Our factories have produced an abundance of goods, but people cannot afford to acquire all the essentials they need. When they do so it is only by means of instalment buying, which is nothing more than mortgaging most of their future earnings to pay for the things they need today. The problem then, in my opinion, is one of the interchangeability of goods, distribution, marketing, and purchasing power. Since the accepted medium of exchange is essentially money, in some form or other, the problem is one' of finance.
I am not saying that all our fiscal policies are wrong. I am saying that many of them are only temporary solutions, since the very problem they try to solve remains unsolved and is becoming more serious all the time. Since monetary science performs an important function in modern society, I propose that in this session of parliament we set up a council of research to undertake a comprehensive study into all the factors of production, exchange, prices, consumption of goods and services. I grant that this would not provide all the answers to our problems. There are many unforeseeable factors that enter into such problems. The findings of such a research council, I do believe, could have historical significance and might well establish a solid and a secure background for sound fiscal policy formulation.
The terms of reference of such a research council should be all-embracing, and in my opinion very similar to the terms of reference given to the national survey of potential product capacity in the United States, an organization of 60 technicians and economists which was financed by the United States government in 1934 for the purpose of discovering: first, the ratio of actual production to capacity production; second, the manpower required for (a) existing production (b) capacity production; third, the degree of interdependence among industries to ascertain possible bottlenecks in the flow of materials from the natural resources to the ultimate consumer; and fourth, what purchasing power would be necessary to command capacity operation of the existing plant, at any given price level.

The Address-Mr. Holowach
It is interesting to note that the national survey of potential product capacity was also empowered to translate capacity production into consumer goods and services, and translate the consumption of these goods and services into terms of life (a) for society; and, (b) for the individual.
The royal commission appointed last year for the purpose of investigating the economic prospects of Canada's future was certainly a step in the right direction, and it had the support of all members of parliament. Its terms of reference, however, limit its study to economic potential and development and not, as I understand it, to the distribution of that potential.
We all approve the setting up of the national research council and various boards to study the natural sciences. Would not a major research project investigating the field of monetary and social science be equally important? Professor C. L. Barber, assistant professor of economics at the University of Manitoba, concluded his article on Canada's economic prospects, appearing in the autumn edition of the Queen's Quarterly, 1955, with these words:
The truth of the matter is, of course, that economists do not have the data they need to determine how long our present prosperity will last. While they understand a good deal more about the way our economic system operates than they did in 1930, very little research has been done on the vital question of what determines our economy's capital requirements. I know of no major research project that has investigated or is currently investigating the relation between population growth and the demand for capital. And the relationship of technological progress to capital requirements is still largely unexplored. The analysis of capital requirements has been listed as one of the topics which the new royal commission on Canada's economic prospects intends to explore. But in the time at their disposal they can hardly more than scratch the surface of this important topic. If our government in Ottawa can find $300,000 to finance the hasty and forced research that is inevitably produced by a royal commission, it can scarcely afford not to set aside funds to finance a long-range program of economic research. Canada badly needs a program of research in the social science field that is the counterpart of that provided by the national research council for the natural sciences. Until the results of such a research program are available economists can do little more than guess at the answer to my initial question..
I should like to turn at this time to a few specific sectors of our economy. The total figures of our gross national production and disposable income make it clear that we are enjoying a high level of prosperity, but there are facts behind the figures which indicate that very many people do not share in that prosperity. I think the lesson to be learned is that the mere fact of an increase in the gross production is not sufficient in

itself for real prosperity unless that production is accompanied by government policies that make possible the consumption of that production.
I believe it is time to talk straight, and this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne is the place to do it. Every member in this house fully understands the value of our agriculture and the wonderful contribution that is being made by farmers of our country in the production of food. The number of speeches that have been made on the subject is an indication of that understanding.
In my own province, farm products exceed Alberta oil and coal wealth. Those of us living in urban constituencies know that the farmer not only feeds us, but we also rely on him buying the services of our city merchants and the products of our workers. Consequently the decline in his farm cash income affects all of us. Let me give one single example of this effect on heavy industry. This is taken from the dominion bureau of statistics news notes of October 28, 1955:
Less harvesting machinery sold. Canadian farmers bought only $26,194,827 worth of new harvesting machinery last year, 62-4 per cent less than in 1953 when the wholesale value of sales totalled $69,579,783.
Just how serious the cash drop has been is further shown in the latest figures released by the dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin, volume 25, No. 14, Friday, January 20, 1956, as follows:
Cash income from the sale of farm products and from participation payments on previous years' prairie grain crops in 1955 amounted to an estimated $2,323,330,000, 2-3 per cent below the 1954 estimate of $2,377,800,000 and 18-5 per cent below the all-time high of $2,849,300,000 in 1952.
This means that farmers have suffered a loss of $526 million of revenue in 1955 as compared with revenues received in 1952. It does seem very peculiar that in a world in which hundreds of millions of people are threatened by starvation and when even in a great producing country such as Canada there are many people who have not enough to eat, our farmers should be forced into economic uncertainty. Here in this very city of Ottawa one sees posters appealing for donations to buy food for hungry children in distant lands, and pictures of children with puffed-up stomachs.
The point I make is that methods must be found to see that our farmer is paid cash, and methods must also be designed so that those nations that require our food are able to get it, irrespective of whether they have gold or dollars.
My second point is that whether we have a poor wheat crop or a bumper harvest,

farmers just never get a square deal. Long before this time the government entered into an arrangement with the farmers. The farmer was to produce; the government was to sell. Let us ask ourselves, who has broken that contract? Mr. Speaker, this government cannot escape answering to the western farmers for their omissions. As a matter of fact the farmers' problems have never been solved by the Liberal government, with the one exception of wartime financing when there was a greatly increased domestic and foreign demand created by the havoc of war. Even at this late hour, when the farmers are united in protest, the government has nothing better to offer them than legislation which, while it may assist some, carries with it far too much liability because it is an open invitation to the farmer to get into debt. It is not debt the farmer wants for having produced a great abundance of the very staff of life, bread; it is a fair cash return for a job well done.
Fortunately there are brighter sides to the picture. The decline in the number of unemployed is perhaps one of the best pieces of news we have heard thus far. It is good news in comparison with the situation a few months ago. We recall that unemployment had reached the top figure of 633,000 last March. It is presently claimed that our current unemployment figure in Canada is slightly over 200,000, and that this figure is normal. Certainly unemployment is never normal for a person who wants a job and cannot find one, and it is certainly not normal for the family that depends upon the earnings of that person.
I submit that the undertaking of one project alone would solve the present unemployment situation. The urgency of a trans-Canada highway system to meet the requirements of western Canada merits attention at this time. It was my privilege to have spoken on this matter in previous sessions, at which time I referred to the desirability of the federal government assisting the various provincial governments in the building of a road from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast by way of Saskatoon, Edmonton, Jasper park and the Yellowhead route. We have consistently asked for that consideration. The other day the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Yuill) also stressed the importance of the Yellowhead route.
All that is needed is a little action from the Liberal government. The federal government's expenditures on highways is completely out of line with the income it receives from the various industries associated with good roads. The provincial governments have a big enough job building their own local and 67509-32 i
The Address-Mr. Holowach marketing roads without having the additional burden of constructing throughways and possible defence roads.
I should like to say how pleased I was to see that we will be considering new legislation on housing. This will, I am sure, contribute much to the elimination of poverty and slum conditions in which juvenile delinquency thrives and which impair the health of our people.
There is one other area in which there is a very great need. During my visit home it was my pleasure to meet with many of the old age pensioners in my constituency and to address their society in Edmonton. In numerous meetings with them I have learned to understand more fully the many extremely difficult problems they face because of the inadequacy of their pensions and the high cost of living. They impress me in other ways, too. I found them to be one of the most alert and thoughtful groups of citizens in our country. They are alert to what is happening in parliament, and they are thoughtful of the difficulties involved in the furtherance of aid to them by governments. Their case is very strong. Because I believe in it, I think it is proper for me to focus the attention of hon. members on it. It is true we have come a long way together in the field of social security legislation, and we are all grateful for that. Equally true is the fact that those on fixed incomes, such as old age pensioners, veterans, the blind and handicapped and all low income groups, are struggling desperately to make ends meet in the face of rising costs.
If everything else in our economy had remained static, perhaps their claim for additional help would be less justified. However, this is not the case at the present time. The production of our country is moving substantially upward, and it is not unreasonable to expect that this prosperity be reflected in improved welfare of the aged and others.
In January, 1951, when the federal old age security pension was made effective, the national income and national production in our country at that time must certainly have had a bearing on the amount this government earmarked for the senior citizens. Since that date the national income and the value of the gross national product have risen by over $2 billion in each category. This would work out to an average increase in income of over $120 for every man, woman and child in Canada.
We hear a great deal of talk from various hon. members regarding the need for markets. I have always maintained that one of the best markets we could have is right here in our own country, our own people. If this market

The Address-Mr. Holowach
is to be used the purchasing power of the people must be increased in the same ratio as our production. If we weigh the problem carefully we see that elementary mathematics are on the side of the demand for an increase of at least $10 for old age pensioners. This would merely mean placing the present pension with the addition of $10 in the same ratio as the pension they received in 1951. As I see it, social justice is also on their side, because after all what is our job if not to devise policies which will alleviate the burdens of the people and fairly distribute increased bounty amongst every level of the Canadian people.
I think the same principle applies to the blind of our country. Just a few days ago I received a letter from the Canadian National Institute for the Blind written by Mr. W. E. Milton, assistant superintendent of the western division, and by Mr. A. DeCoursey, chairman of the Alberta division of the Canadian Council of the Blind, which reads as follows:
Last year, in response to representations by the C.N.I.B. and The Canadian Council of the Blind, parliament amended the Blind Persons Act to lower the qualifying age for blindness allowance to 18 and to slightly raise the means test ceilings on allowable income. We greatly appreciated your support of these amendments and your interest in the welfare of the blind.
Further to the letter you recently received from our national headquarters, we are writing to urge your support of our current one-point legislative objective. This important objective, a federal allowance without means test to all blind Canadians over and above the existing maintenance allowance to help meet the unavoidable expense of blindness, was advocated but not implemented last year. It is explained in the attached pamphlet and continues to be an urgent need. The principle of such an allowance is endorsed by the United Nations and by the world council for the welfare of the blind, and is in effect in some countries.
You will be interested to learn that, at March 31, 1955, the blind population of Canada exceeded 21,000 persons. Only 7,570 of these were in receipt of the blindness allowance. Approximately 1,400 were too young to qualify while 7,344 were 70 and over and therefore, in receipt of the old age security pension. The remainder about 5,000 were ineligible for various reasons including inability to qualify under the rigid means test which limits a single person to an annual income including the allowance of $960 and a married person to $1,560.
It will be obvious that the unavoidable expense of blindness is a real concern to every blind adult regardless of whether he qualifies or not for the maintenance allowance provided by the Blind Persons Act. Present legislation ignores his blindness if he is employed, but the unusual expense of blindness continues. Present legislation ignores his blindness when he reaches 70 and recognizes only his age. We, who know the need, earnestly solicit your support of our reasonable aim.
With appreciation for past courtesies and best wishes for 1956, we remain.
There are a few signs of warning that we should heed. The debt in which people find themselves is at an all-time high. I believe that most hon. members who read the local
papers will have seen the report in yesterday's Ottawa Journal which was captioned "Consumer Credit Up $305,000,000" and which read as follows:
Consumer credit ballooned during the third quarter of 1955 to $2,212,000,000, up $305,000,000 from the first quarter of the year.
The taxation policies of this government make it virtually impossible for people to save and put away a little bit for a rainy day. I urge this government to make tax reductions, especially for the relief of those in the lower income brackets. It is a complete fallacy to claim that government revenue would decline. The very reverse is true, because reduced taxes would increase purchasing power in the hands of the people which in turn would stimulate consumption, investment and production. Consequently in the end our government would benefit by a greater increase in our economy.
In carrying out our program let us continue to guard against what I consider to be a real danger, namely the growth of the bigger and bigger government, which means more centralization and bureaucracy. There is far too much of that even now, and our efforts should be to reverse the trend. I think one way to do it would be to decentralize decisions as much as possible, and make available to every level of government adequate finances to enable it to do a good job.
The failure of the last two federal-provincial conferences, one in April and one in October, to my mind was a result of the government's refusal to do that very thing. There is more truth than fiction in the statement that Ottawa continues to attempt to create the impression that they are doing the provinces a favour by giving back to them a small share of the provinces' income. In the present crisis of outside events, when we need unity more than anything else, I think it is inexcusible for this government to continue hogging everything.
I think decentralization could be brought about in many other fields, such as the fields of aviation, radio and television. Why should the government have monopolies in these fields and then ask the taxpayer to foot the bill? Would it not be more sensible for us to bring about the desired expansion in these fields by inviting various voluntary and private organizations to enter them? There is every indication that there are many such organizations which would like to do so. There would be a double effect; on the one hand we would have the expanded services which are required, and on the other hand the cost of such expansion would not necessarily fall upon the shoulders of the Canadian taxpayer.
IMr. Holowach.]

On previous occasions I have drawn to the attention of responsible ministers the need of a post office building in Beverly, Alberta. I examined the situation several times last autumn, and I can honestly say that the facilities are deplorably inadequate. In view of the requests made by their member in numerous debates the public there have a right to know why this government is still ignoring their request. I think these people are entitled to have a public building in which satisfactory post office premises would be available. Through me they once again respectfully draw the attention of the new minister to their need.
In conclusion may I just join with others in my constituency and elsewhere and ask in all sincerity that this government, which is charged with the responsibility for making decisions, do so solely in the light of objective thought and respond to the observations on some of the problems which I have briefly outlined.

Mr. Speaker, there are a few things I should like to discuss briefly. Yesterday I was at home in my riding of Queens, and while there I met with and talked to a great number of people. I met and talked with many more during the last weeks and months of 1955. There are many things about which my people are happy, but there are several things which are causing concern and I should like to mention two of them.
Our provincial economy is largely dependent upon agriculture. While Canada as a whole is prosperous and booming, that is not true of agriculture in our province. This industry has experienced comparatively difficult times. Potatoes constitute only one phase of our agricultural economy, but they are the main cash crop of many farmers. They provide the extra cash which pays outstanding bills and provides the means to make purchases for the home or for the farm plant. You know as well as I do that when our farmers have cash to spend the urban centres benefit. Charlottetown, the capital city, is in the centre of my riding, surrounded by rural areas.
Right now the question of a tariff on potatoes is causing concern in my area. This matter was the subject of an intensive inquiry during the past summer by the tariff board, whose hearings in Ottawa I attended. Members of the board visited various parts of Canada and talked to producers and shippers and investigated the industry as a whole pretty thoroughly. I was glad to hear during the last day or two from the Minister of Finance that this problem is going to be studied further in the near future.
The Address-Mr. Matheson
The change last year in the Unemployment Insurance Act has caused considerable difficulty at home. Our office advises that as a result of one of the changes made, approximately one-third of those eligible previously for benefits were ineligible last fall. I believe I was one of the first in Canada to draw this problem to the attention of the Minister of Labour, who happened to be in my area early last fall when I discussed the matter with him. I have discussed it further with him since coming to Ottawa. I know that other areas face the same problem, and I hope those responsible can effect a solution. I see no reason why they cannot.
I want to thank the Minister of Labour for having come to my constituency at that time, and also I want to thank the Minister of Finance who was in our province yesterday, when he spoke to several meetings. I feel quite sure that the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Fisheries, the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacNaught), would want to associate his name with what I am saying, as he was there with us.
The hon. member for Prince had a most unhappy experience recently, when his constituency was hit extremely hard by a severe sleet storm. The western part of my riding was also affected adversely, and as a result there are many people who will not have their electric power restored for several weeks. But the entire area of Prince took the brunt of the storm, and they have had and are having extremely difficult times. They are still having difficulty, and it will continue for some time to come. I want to express my sympathy to those who are so very seriously handicapped by the loss of service and the crippling disruptions that loss entails.
Yesterday, while in Charlottetown, I talked to the manager of our local employment office. He was very happy, he told me, about the manner in which business firms and people generally are co-operating in the very fine effort his office is making to stir up interest in providing extra winter employment for people who would otherwise be idle. I know he would like me to put his appreciation on record today.
I spoke a few minutes ago about some of the economic difficulties we have in our area. I regret the manner in which some of the members opposite approach the problems of the maritimes. I say that because I do not think we can get anywhere by just being belligerent. My own idea is that we should seek to attract listeners and get their attention.
It is true that other parts of Canada have prospered beyond the fondest dreams of some of the people in our area. They have

The Address-Mr. Matheson advantages of geographic location. They are close to large centres of population. This means good markets. They are close to sources of abundant power which is available at a cost that makes it economically feasible to use that power in industry. They have many advantages, and I recognize that.
I bow to no one in my loyalty to my own area, but our lack of progress perhaps may not all be the fault of someone else or some other place. In my own personal experience I have found one cannot advance just by pushing somebody else down. You have to climb the rungs of the ladder yourself if you are going to ascend. In this connection I am very happy to note that the Atlantic provinces economic council is a most live and active organization in our area. It is generally known as APEC and is composed of some of the best men in our provinces. They are probing and searching for ways and means to advance our interests, to promote new and better industries and to improve and extend, if possible, the ones we now have.
If I may state their object in a few words it is this: self-help for the provinces in which they are working. A number of men from my own province are working with that organization. I do not mean we shall not accept and, indeed, seek help and economic assistance from the federal government in an effort to improve our position. I have in mind now a project that would be of tremendous benefit to us in Prince Edward Island. I think it would also be a boon to some of the adjacent provinces, particularly New Brunswick. It would practically revolutionize our transportation facilities so far as connection with the mainland is concerned.
We have a modern and powerful icebreaking car ferry. We have a second stand-by boat that is now over 40 years old. These ships render a good service to the extent that their facilities enable them to do so, but there are times when their facilities are not capable of handling the traffic that is offering. At best the delays are annoying to the tourist, and they are very costly to the industrialist and the businessman. If one misses a boat he may have to wait several hours for the next one.
The proposal I have in mind would end these delays and would assure us of continuous communication with the mainland as was envisioned in the pact of confederation. I am proposing a causeway across the strait of Northumberland. Before someone tells me this is fantastic or even economically unsound, let me say that the proposal has received and is now receiving the very serious attention of people who are qualified


to consider and discuss such things. I cannot give any details, because the knowledge I have of details is knowledge given to me in confidence for the moment. I can say, however, that preliminary studies of the project indicate that the proposal may well be feasible from an economic standpoint and is entirely feasible from an engineering standpoint.
Several firms qualified to study such things have been looking into the possibilities. Included among them is one of the most highly regarded causeway engineers on this continent. May I suggest that the annual deficit on the operations of the car ferries on the Borden-Tormentine run would finance the cost of construction. By that I mean it would pay the interest on the money it would take to build the causeway.
The distance across this strip of water is much greater than across the strait of Canso, where a causeway was built and is now in efficient operation. On the other hand the water is not nearly as deep. Certainly the development would be most desirable in so far as the improved service that would be rendered is concerned. There would hardly be any comparison between the service that would be available and what is available now.
A causeway would translate into terms of modern development and modern thinking the pledge of confederation to provide continuous communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. Some might say it would join Prince Edward Island to Canada. I should like to say that it would join Canada to Prince Edward Island.

speechtext:
In a paragraph in the speech from the throne I was pleased to note that the royal commission to examine and report upon our economic prospects is proceeding with its inquiry. I am hoping they will recommend for one thing the decentralization of industry in this country. It is something we in the maritimes have asked for on many occasions,

The Address-Mr. Brooks and it is something in which this federal government could have given us a good lead in connection with the matter of defence production. It is also something which I believe would have been economically and militarily sound.
Another paragraph in the speech from the throne states as follows, as reported at page 2 of Hansard:
Canada has enjoyed, on the whole, a high level of prosperity. Some sectors of the economy have not fully participated in this increased well-being.
It is also a statement of fact, Mr. Speaker, that in certain sections of this country there has been a high level of prosperity. However, we in the maritime provinces have not enjoyed that prosperity, although we are pleased that other sections of the country have done so. This has been true not only for this year but for a great many years in our part of the world.
The people who today are suffering the most and who have the greatest problems are the farmers of the dominion. We have in this country today great surpluses of wheat, of butter and of apples. We cannot sell our apples, as a matter of fact, and we have a surplus of potatoes. I sometimes wonder what would happen if potatoes and apples were non-perishable goods, as are wheat and butter. If they were non-perishable, in addition to having millions of bushels of wheat and millions of pounds of butter stored up in this country I am satisfied that we would have millions of bushels of apples and millions of bushels of potatoes.
This is a great problem for the Dominion of Canada. The fact that we cannot export or sell our goods is a greater problem for us than for any other country in the world. In order to live, Canada must export from 20 to 25 per cent of her goods. In the United States 95 per cent of the production is consumed there. Hence the problem, so far as they are concerned, is not the great one that it is for us.
I am not going to discuss wheat this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, because I know little about that problem. I know a little bit more about butter. In my constituency of Royal, particularly in the county of Kings, we are a dairy-producing section. We have some of the finest dairy herds you will find anywhere, not only in the maritime provinces but in Canada. My town of Sussex is known as the dairy centre of the maritime provinces. In the town of Sussex we have two large and well-run butter factories.
The fact that it is not possible for Canada to sell all her butter ere ites a serious problem


in my section of the country. I know there are many young men today who say this: If the future of the dairy industry and the butter industry does not get any brighter, I shall have to give up the farm or leave the farm that my father worked for years, leave the herds of cattle which it has taken so many years to improve, and find work in some other part of the country.
Just recently we were honoured in the province of New Brunswick by having held there a meeting of the dairy farmers of Canada. We were pleased indeed to have this convention held in the city of Saint John on the 14th day of this month. I might say that it is the first time this convention has ever been held in the maritime provinces. To have these men representing 455,000 producers meet in our province was a great compliment to us and, I believe, a great inspiration.
I was pleased to read in the paper the objectives of the dairy farmers of Canada. They are as follows:
With their primary objective "To promote the betterment of the dairy industry, and to co-operate with all organizations to this end," the dairy farmers of Canada have many other aims. They endeavour to maintain and improve the high quality of Canadian dairy foods; to encourage the adoption of uniform grade standards; to promote research by recognized government and other established agencies, and to develop markets, lower production costs and generally benefit the industry and the consumer.
These are laudable objectives, and I am sure we wish the dairy farmers every success.
I am not one who would try to prescribe a solution for the present situation. I have always felt that our farm products should have greater sale in Great Britain. Before the war we had a great market in Great Britain, particularly for our apples, wheat and cheese. Had some effort been made to try to develop this market further since the last war, I believe that we would not have in Canada today such large surpluses of wheat and of butter.
By the way, I might say this. When one reads the press it is extremely confusing to note that while, according to an answer received from the minister's department, there is in Canada a surplus of some 100 million pounds of butter, nevertheless the Minister of Agriculture says that there is no surplus. It is very difficult indeed to reconcile statements of that kind. So far as I am concerned, and I believe so far as the people of Canada are concerned, they are going to believe the statements put out by the bureau of statistics.

Another complaint which the dairy farmers have, and which I feel is a very just complaint, is that we are using too much vegetable oil in this country. Many times in my own constituency I have heard it said that some effort should be made to curtail the large quantity of vegetable oils being used today. I understand that vegetable oils which are imported into Canada are the basis for margarine. In an address to the national dairy council at Lake Louise on September 5, the president of the council had this to say:
It may be noted in this connection that our good neighbours across our southern border are this year anticipating a record crop of soy beans. The price of soy beans has already dropped drastically, and is reflected in recent large price reductions of margarine in Canada. In other words, our dairy farmers are being exposed to price competition from foreign produced oils in large surplus supply, without benefit of any effective tariff and without any attempt being made to meet the competition in the only way the consumer will recognize, namely, price.
It is ironic that the consumer demand for cheaper food which comes largely from foreign sources, is undermining the prosperity of a large segment of our producers of basic raw products and thereby also undermining the prosperity of these same consumers.
As I said a moment ago I think the dairy farmers have a very just cause for complaint in this connection.
I have been quite interested in the speeches made by hon. members from my own province. I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska upon his maiden speech. He gives every indication of being a very courageous and valuable member of this house. I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, a young member who is certainly taking his place in this House of Commons. I congratulate the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton. I doubt if there is anyone in the house who understands the problems of the potato producer in Canada better than this hon. member.
I should like to say a few words with reference to some matters which were brought up by hon. members opposite. The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy) again mentioned the Chignecto canal. The hon. member knows my attitude on this subject. The Chignecto canal is something which was discussed in this house long before the hon. member for Wetmorland ever had any connection with politics. I recall my old friend Mr. Black, the former member for Cumberland, speaking on this matter many years ago. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) has spoken on it on many occasions, and I have done the same. I do not believe there was ever a time in the history of New Brunswick when the Chignecto canal meant more to the people than it does now.
The Address-Mr. Brooks
I shall not weary the house by reading it, but in 1949 when we were discussing the St. Lawrence seaway I made a speech in which I said that if the St. Lawrence seaway were developed, we in the province of New Brunswick were prepared to pay our full share of the cost of this development. However, the only practical benefit we could receive would be through building the Chignecto canal, which I consider to be supplementary to the St. Lawrence seaway. It would mean a reduction of over 400 miles in the carrying of freight from Saint John, New Brunswick, the bay of Fundy or ports along the New England coast. I do not see how the federal government, when it goes on with the development of this St. Lawrence seaway, can neglect the Chignecto canal.
But I want to say to the hon. member for Westmorland

and the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Lusby) who also mentioned it-if they had been here five or six years ago when a delegation came from the maritime provinces, representatives from all parts of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and had seen the brush-off those men received from this government in the railway committee room they would feel, as I feel, that if the Chignecto canal is ever built it will have to be built by some other government than the present one. The Conservative party has been in favour of the Chignecto canal ever since it was mentioned here a number of years ago.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is another subject about which I should like to speak for a few minutes, and that is Passamaquoddy. Before I do so, I want to say to the hon. member for Charlotte that I was very much surprised at what seemed to me to be an attack on the Beechwood project here this afternoon. We do not expect that Beechwood will be the answer to all our problems so far as hydro development is concerned. It will hardly more than carry the load over the next eight or ten years. It is not necessary in the development of Beechwood, as the hon. member knows, that we obtain storage rights in Quebec or Maine. If the full development of the Saint John river is ever undertaken, then it will be necessary to obtain such rights. However, so far as Beechwood is concerned, the storage we have in the province of New Brunswick alone will give a waterhead sufficient for the development of this project. When the hon. member tries to draw a red herring across the Beechwood project by saying we must obtain authority from Maine and Quebec, he is making a statement which he knows is incorrect.
Now, so far as the 'Quoddy development is concerned, that has been advocated for a good many years. There is a long history to

The Address-Mr. Brooks the proposed development of tidal power on the Passamaquoddy river. I recall that when I was a member of the provincial legislature some years ago a man by the name of Dexter Cooper, one of the leading hydroelectric engineers in the world, came before us with a model for the proposed development of hydroelectric power from the rise and fall of the tide in the Passamaquoddy river. He explained it to the members then, but there was not much interest in New Brunswick at that time. As a matter of fact the reception was rather lukewarm.
Then the depression came and after that the war, and there was very little interest taken in the proposal except in the United States. President Roosevelt was very much interested in it. He had lived during the summer months on Campobello island near the Passamaquoddy, so he knew the possibilities of developing hydroelectric power there. He was in favour of it as was his successor, President Truman. The state of Maine has been able to interest not only the House of Representatives and the Senate of the United States, but they have been able to get congress to vote money for further investigation into this development.
Stated briefly, I believe this development is feasible. I believe also that if it is developed, and if the province of New Brunswick and the Dominion of Canada will share in the development and the province of New Brunswick is able to get its full share of the horsepower, which is considered to be about a million-New Brunswick's share would probably be about 450,000 horsepower-New Brunswick would be placed on a par with any other province in this Dominion of Canada so far as electric power is concerned, and we would have sufficient power for any industries that might wish to come to our province in the future.
As I said a moment ago, there was indifference in the past, and I am afraid that at Washington they still think there is indifference on the part of the people of Canada, represented, of course, by this government.
I received a letter dated February 9, 1953, from Senator Margaret Smith, of Maine. That is nearly three years ago. The matter was then being brought up at Washington by Senator Smith. Her letter reads:
Dear Mr. Brooks:
Washington is very interested in the Quoddy proposal. However, there is a general impression here that Canada has a relatively negative attitude on the proposal-
I sometimes wonder whether that is true.
I hope it is not, Mr. Speaker. I hope this government will do everything it possibly can to prove whether or not it is a feasible proposition. If it is proved feasible, I hope 
the government will do everything it possibly can to develop this great waterpower.
I continue to quote:

Enclosed is a copy of the current legislation. The Maine delegation has a conference set for this coming Tuesday morning to talk with President Eisenhower on the proposal.
Thank you for your generous comments about my senatorial record. I have a real affection for our neighbour Canada and enjoy every opportunity I have to go to Canada.
Sincerely yours,
Margaret Smith.
There is another matter which I had intended to mention briefly, but it has been well discussed by the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. White), the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), and others. I refer to veterans affairs. I was disappointed that no mention of veterans was made in the speech from the throne this year. They should have been mentioned. There are problems. The other day the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Balcom) mentioned the war veterans allowance ceilings, and suggested that they should be raised to $1,200 for single veterans and $2,000 for married veterans. Members of the committee know that last year and other years I had amendments and resolutions to this effect.
The senior hon. member for Halifax mentioned service in England. I should like to say to the hon. member for Halifax that for the past 15 years, ever since the War Veterans Allowance Act has been discussed either in committee or in this House of Commons, opposition members and our party in particular have pressed for the inclusion of the soldiers who served in England under the war veterans allowance. It has been turned down repeatedly by his own party. I assure him that if he ever expects these men to be included under the terms of the War Veterans Allowance Act he will have to look to some party other than his own to take the initiative.
Certain amendments to the Pension Act should be considered this year as well. Since I am speaking of veterans affairs, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief reference to a trip I made overseas this year in company with the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness). First I want to thank the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney), for the kindness they showed in making the arrangements for us to visit the cemeteries in France, Holland, Belgium and Italy.
At the outset may I say there is a mistaken idea, not only among our own people but among people of other nations, that those

cemeteries are cared for and looked after by the people of the different countries in which they are located. That is not true. I read in the visitors' books of many of the cemeteries that some persons from Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Great Britain, who had visited the cemeteries, had written in the following remarks: "We are grateful to the people of Holland", or "We are grateful to the people of France", or Belgium, "for the care they are taking of our soldiers' graves."
Nothing could be further from the fact, Mr. Speaker. These graves are being cared for by the imperial war graves commission. This is an organization that was set up in 1917. The head of it is the Duke of Gloucester. There are representatives from all of the countries of the commonwealth. They have a tremendous task to perform. They care for the graves of 1,104,000 men who died in the first war and 569,000 who died in the second war. Their activities extend to Africa, Asia, Europe and wherever commonwealth or British Empire soldiers are buried.
I was amazed and pleased; I can hardly find adjectives to describe the manner in which those graves and cemeteries are looked after. There could not be any finer cemeteries anywhere in the world than the cemeteries that are being looked after by the imperial war graves commission. In those graves you will find lying side by side men from all parts of the commonwealth and the British Empire, soldiers from Australia, New Zealand, Canada, India, South Africa, or wherever they may have come from. The resting places of our dead are places of beauty and peace. On every grave you will see flowers, rose bushes, or shrubs of some kind blooming.
If any hon. member has an opportunity to visit Europe, I suggest that he go and see for himself. It would be impossible for him to visit all the cemeteries, because it would take weeks. The hon. member for Calgary North and I spent three weeks there and we did not see nearly all the cemeteries. None of them is truly Canadian, but those that approach the nearest to being Canadian and are called Canadian are at Beny-sur-Mer, Bretteville-sur-Laize, Dieppe, Calais, Bergen op Zoom, Cassino and Ortona in Italy.
In addition to visiting the graves we visited the memorials. The Canadian memorial at Vimy Ridge is probably the finest memorial of any nation in the world. I was a little concerned to read in the press not long ago an account of the visit to this memorial of Captain Sharpe of the 1st Canadian division. He went there on November 11 expecting to find a ceremony of some kind, and was very
The Address-Mr. Brooks much surprised to find that only he and the caretaker visited the memorial on that occasion. The caretaker presented him with a wreath and asked him to place it on the memorial, which he was very proud and happy to do. Upon his return to Canada he wrote an article and expressed surprise tha1 a ceremony was not held at Vimy Ridge or November 11. I am sure this information must come as a surprise to a great manj people and I think it is a matter that should be very carefully looked into.
Another memorial in which I am particularly interested is the Newfoundland memorial in Belgium, and I want to congratulate the people of Newfoundland for arranging for this splendid memorial. It is perhaps the most practical memorial of any I saw. It consists of 100 acres of land which have beer left in the same state they were in following the war; that is, there are trenches, shell hole: and machine gun emplacements there whicl present a realistic picture of battle condi tions. There is just one thing I might criti cize in relation to this memorial; that is th< caretaker's home, which is in a state o disrepair. I think some attention should bi given to it.
