Mr. Speaker, at the outset of this speech, I should like to congratulate the movers of the address in reply (Mrs. Shipley and Mr. Laflamme) on the way they handled their task.
The hon. member for Timiskaming pointed out various matters of great concern to her on behalf of her constituency and, as it is the first time that a member of the fair sex moves the address in reply, she deserves the compliments that have been extended to her by the members of this house.
The young and new member for Belle-chasse also deserves congratulations from his colleagues, and I do hope that he will often take part in the debates which will be held in this house.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, in the time I have at my disposal I intend to speak on two subjects which will no doubt be the subject of many discussions in this house and throughout Canada in the years to come. Automation and free enterprise have been responsible for many discussions, and I should like to express my views thereon.
During the past year or so people have oecome aware of a new word. They have already become familiar with such terms as atomic energy, radar, and microwave for :elevision and electronics. Now they hear and read about automation and a few of us ook forward to the great new things that automation will mean to the world. Others are worried and fearful and think it will aring about unemployment and poverty.
Just what is automation, and what does t mean to us all? Automation is really aothing new. It is just the continuation of a long, long process of technological advance, t really began a way back when man first nvented the lever to help him to lift a leavy object, and it continued through all he ages as man sought to make his daily vork easier and his production greater.
For a long time no one feared these mprovements in working tools because they ould see how helpful they were. Then, ibout a century ago, men invented machines

that could do much of the work they had had to do. They began using steam to provide the power that had formerly been created by man's muscles. Then they used water power to make electricity.
This brought about what was called the industrial revolution. Machines, it was found, could knit yarns and make it unnecessary for thousands of women and children to work in the knitting mills. Machines could do more in less time and work became easier.
People were frightened then, too, because they thought the machine would do them out of jobs. Some of them went so far as to smash the machinery, thinking it was a job thief. But the machines did not make unemployment. They created new employment. Thousands of people had new jobs at higher pay, making the machines. Working conditions were improved. The things the machines made cost less to produce, so more people could buy them. And as more people bought them there were new jobs in the mills and new jobs making the machines, delivering and selling the goods they produced. Everybody was better off than they had ever been before.
During this century we have seen even greater advances in mechanization. Nobody would want to go back to the days of hand work, when everybody worked long hours for poor pay and were unable even to buy the things they produced. How many people could own their own homes today if all our houses were built as they were in the past? In those days, home building could be done only during the summer. Plasterers and bricklayers, masons and roofers worked only six months a year. Everything was done by hand, from the digging of cellars to the laying of shingles.
Then technological improvements began in the building trades. Mehanical shovels dug out excavations in a matter of hours instead of days. Electrical welders went to work. Building materials were fabricated in the factories. Thousands of houses could be built in a season, and year-round employment was provided for those making components.
The same is true, of course, in many industries. The motor car and the television set are possible only because of mechanization. The telephone and the electric refrigerator would be impossible if they had to be made by hand.
All of us accept these modern things, and when we think of it we realize that we could have none of them without machinery. Every year in research departments and in experimental factories new things are made and new ways are devised for making them. All

this is simply technological development, new advances in the field of technology. And all this helps to make possible our modern way of life.
Now we come back to that new word, automation. It is really just a further step in technological advancement. Certainly it goes far beyond what our forefathers thought could ever happen in our industrial world. The first machines required many men to operate them. Under automation there will be many machines which do all the things the human operators used to do. New machines will work automatically.
The simplest illustration is the automatic gear shift on a new car. It has always been necessary for the driver of a car to change gears when he wanted to stop and start, drive through mud or snow, or speed up or slow down. Now an automatic gear shift does all that for him. The car knows when to change gears and does it all by itself. So we have automation.
In a factory automation will work the same way. At a certain time of day the automatic machinery will start a press or a weaving machine going; it will watch to make sure the machine is operating efficiently, and it will stop the machine when a certain amount of production has been achieved. It will also do such things as test the product from time to time and make sure that nothing is wrong.
So it will not be necessary to have an operator standing guard all the time to keep the machine running. This is what is called a push-button operation; you push a button and the machine does the rest.
What will be the next result of automation? In the first place it will release a number of people from humdrum jobs and enable them to take work with more opportunity. It will do away with the need for common labour and make more jobs for skilled workers. In short it will upgrade our workers, giving them better employment, better working conditions and better pay. At the same time it will reduce our production costs and enable more people to buy the things they want.
Instead of being afraid of automation we should welcome it. It is another step along the road to a more abundant life for everyone. Automation, the word of the future, holds out great promise to us all today. It is part of the brave new world in which we live, and is something our children will accept as one of our great contributions to their happiness.
So much for automation. Another term which is so often misunderstood is the word enterprise. Many people have misinterpreted this word, many fear it and many praise it.
The Address-Mr. Bourque In the first place, let us admit that there is no such thing in this world as free enterprise, if by free we mean enterprise that is completely beyond any control. In fact none of us would want such a thing. If there were perfectly free enterprise there would be no government, no laws, no control. There would just be chaos. So I think all of us agree that we have enterprise, but it is subject to many laws and conditions which make it acceptable to society.
No individual or company is allowed to carry on an enterprise which is harmful to society. We do not permit the selling of dope or narcotics except under strict medical and governmental supervision. We have imposed certain restrictions on the selling of comic books. We do not permit people to publish libelous statements. In all these respects enterprise is not free.
At the same time I think it is also a mistake to refer to private enterprise. Certainly there are some enterprises that are private, that are carried on by one man or by very few men, but most of our great enterprises in the country are public enterprises in the sense that they are made possible by joint ownership of a great many people. The telephone company, for instance, is owned by hundreds of thousands of shareholders. Every big manufacturing company has many, many shareholders, and so do all our great corporations.
In law we make a distinction between private and public companies. A private company is restricted to a certain number of shareholders, usually less than 50. A public company sells its stock on the market and may have many, many owners. So it is correct to say that our enterprise in Canada is very seldom private. It is usually the result of participation by the public.
We in Canada have been fortunate in devising a method by which enterprise can thrive. We admit the responsibility of the government in certain fields, but in the bulk of our national activities we rely upon the enterprise of those Canadians who seek to build and create and serve their fellows at a profit. We all believe in one form or another of the profit system.
The man who works for wages sells his time and his labour at a profit. He seeks enough for his efforts to enable him to buy the things he wants and do the things he likes to do. He realizes, also, that those who pay him must be able to realize a profit on his services or they will soon be out of business and he will be out of a job. The need for a profit goes all along the line. Our whole economy is based upon the desire and ability of each of us to profit by his own endeavours.

The Address-Mr. Bourque And because this system exists we enjoy the second highest standard of living in the world and are one of the great development countries of the world.
Since the last war Canada has seen the investment of millions of dollars and the employment of hundreds of thousands of people. We are growing, and we are growing quickly, because not only do we have the resources here to develop but we have the right economic and political climate in which to develop them. Nobody wishes to invest his time or his money in something of which he can be deprived without warning. No one wishes to live in a country where his political freedom is constantly in danger.
In Canada neither of these conditions exists. We on this side of the house recognize the need for supervision and control. We realize that in essence all the resources of Canada belong to the people of Canada, and that these people must not be exploited. But we realize also that our resources are of no value unless they are developed, and that in order to develop them we must encourage enterprise and allow it to be rewarded by a profit.
Enterprise in this country recognizes its responsibility to the people. It seeks to provide employment for Canadians and to encourage them to develop their skills and increase their earnings. It endeavours to provide goods and services at reasonable prices, and it maintains strong competition in order to give the public an opportunity to pick and choose. We have on our markets many cars in many models, our banks compete strenuously for customers, and in men's and women's wear we stock our counters with a great variety of styles and colours.
There was a time when some people thought this enterprise system was wasteful. They thought it would be preferable to have only one company and one product in a line; then, they thought, costs would be lower and prices would be cheaper. Now, however, we know that competition leads to lower cost production methods, competition creates new markets, competition lowers prices. That is the fruit of enterprise. More goods of better quality at lower prices all come from our system of letting men freely and honestly seek to improve their products or their services. It has brought us unparalleled prosperity. It has provided work and opportunity for most of our citizens.
Because we are enterprising people, and because we believe in true enterprise that seeks to serve rather than exploit, we in Canada are envied by people in other parts of the globe. Many thousands of people have


come here to live with us, and many more thousands will follow. Some of them come from countries where true enterprise has never existed, or where it has been stamped out by false theorists. Those who have lived where there is no enterprise know what it is to live without freedom. Under our blue skies, in this great expanse of territory, they will find rewards for hard work, for skill, for ingenuity, for perseverance and for courage. This is not an easy land in which to live. It is not a land for weaklings or for people who place security above all else.
Canada has been built upon struggle. We have had to fight against nature. We have been forced to work hard because we are next door to a rich and powerful neighbour. But we have established certain values that have paid us well. We have rich soil waiting to be worked. We have great mineral deposits waiting to be brought out of the rock. We have vast forests and fisheries waiting to be developed. There is room here for men and women with enterprise. They can and will make this country one of the most favoured lands on earth.
Now may I take just a few minutes to talk about the common-sense aspects of economics. Let us look at the situation on this continent and in the world today as it affects us as plain, ordinary, everyday citizens. In Canada today we are enjoying another spurt in what is the greatest boom in history. Everybody and his uncle today are buying motor cars. Almost every home you visit has a television set. Everywhere you look there are new homes under construction, and the furniture companies are just waiting to sell the new owners the furniture to go in them. All this means jobs, higher pay, more vacations and more spending, until it all goes round just like a circle.
The danger is, of course, that in our mad rush to buy new things we may forget some of the other values of life. When you are busy making the payments on a car it is sometimes hard to remember that nobody is calling on the family next door because they happen to belong to another race, have a different religion or speak a different language. Yet surely good neighbourliness is just as important as driving a motor car. Or is it? That is one of the things we should take time to think about, even if it means turning off the radio or the television set.
James Farley, the United States politician, recently pointed out that the United States, with all its prosperity, is losing some of its spiritual wealth. Like everybody else Farley enjoys the good things of life, but he thinks

one of the good things is good behaviour based upon faith and a sense of spiritual values. Perhaps we should all take time out to consider whether or not we are becoming so obsessed with material things that we are forgetting the basic values of our civilization. It sometimes seems strange today to suggest that man cannot live by bread alone. Some cynics laugh and say "No, he needs cake as well". But the truth is that it is spiritual food we need to supplement our bread, not richer material food.
I am not one of those who believe that the world is going to the dogs just because we all have more money to spend and more leisure time in which to spend it. No one, I think, would want to go back to the days of the hungry thirties when a man did not know where his next job was coming from. Prices are high today, but we have the money to pay them. Prices were low back in 1935, but very few people could afford to buy what they needed. The good old days sound wonderful to the old-timers, and sometimes we can even convince the younger generation that it was fun to live in the horse and carriage age, but the truth is that we all have a chance to live better lives today than our parents or our grandparents did 50 or 75 years ago.
Nobody has all the answers. But we can all seek some of them on our own. A United States magazine recently suggested that juvenile delinquency today is a result of our lack of discipline. We try to understand children instead of training them to do right. That is one editor's answer. James Farley says we should pay more attention to spiritual values, and no matter what church we go to or what faith we hold we should seek better understanding there.
Labour unions demand higher wages. Employers say if wages go up prices must rise, too. Consumers, and that includes both labour and employers, sit in the middle, caught either way. To the amateur in economics it is all very confusing. But sometimes the amateurs are smarter than the professionals. Why not have a discussion group in your own families and invite the neighbours in as well to discuss everyday problems? See what you think about these problems and reach your own conclusions. Are we too material? Think it over. You probably have the right answer yourself.

Mr. Speaker, my first words will be of congratulation to the mover (Mrs. Shipley) and the seconder (Mr. Laflamme) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I might say, however, that I am not going to lay it on too thick, because I think there is a saturation point beyond which one must not go since there is always a danger of spoiling people by praising them too much.
Tonight I want to talk about the people in my constituency and the conditions in which they find themselves. I am going to make some criticisms but I am also going to offer some suggestions which, if followed, I think would benefit the people I represent.
I travelled in my constituency during the recess and logged some 10,000 miles. I talked to a great number of people about their problems, and I think I know something about them. One of the last of my constituents whom I saw before coming to Ottawa was a man I met on the streets of Saskatoon. He said to me, "I hope you people down there will be able to do something to alleviate the conditions that we are experiencing at the present time." Tonight it is my purpose to try to do just that. I want to try to do something that will help the people whom I represent.
First of all may I say that I deplore the fact that some of the members in this chamber and at least one of the cabinet ministers have played down the real situation existing in the wheat-growing areas of western Canada. I have lived in that country for over 50 years. I homesteaded there and went through all the pioneering stages. Never since the hungry thirties, and not even then, have I seen a greater scarcity of money. The situation then was not much worse than it is at the present time. The whole plea of the population in that whole area is this: Try to get some money in the pockets of the farmers.
During this debate most of the talk has been centred around the farmers' need for cash and certainly their need is great, because their costs of operation have been going up steadily and their income has been going down rapidly. Not only have farmers come to me; never before have so many businessmen come to see me to ask if something could not be done to get money into the hands of the farmers.
The farmers are in this position. Last year they had a small crop of extremely poor quality, and they received little money for it. The result was that many of the merchants in the smaller towns advanced credit.

The Address-Mr. Campbell Those merchants are obliged to pay cash for the things which they sell on credit. Many of these merchants are in the position of not being able to meet their commitments and of not knowing how long they are going to be able to carry on. They are almost in a worse position than are the farmers because they have rent to pay, help to pay and so forth and so on. I therefore deprecate the fact that at least one cabinet minister has played down the situation there.
I may also say that I attended many meetings of farmers. Those meetings were attended not only by farmers but by businessmen, heads of boards of trade and so on. They all asked for one thing, namely that the government should make an advance payment to farmers for grain stored on the farm. I am not going to spend any time belabouring that point, because the government and this house has decided that that is not going to be done. But as I said before, I deplore the fact that at least one minister of the crown has played down the real situation that exists in that country.
I read now an extract from the Globe and Mail of January 24 reporting what happened when the Minister of Agriculture was speaking in the city of Winnipeg. According to the extract this is what he said:
Agriculture Minister Gardiner said today that farmers are not as hard up "as some people would try to have us believe."
I think the minister is playing down the actual situation. I am going to say this. If there were an election tomorrow, neither the Minister of Agriculture nor any other Liberal would be back here from Saskatchewan. I have never seen the people as angry as they are now over the lack of action on the part of this government in the present situation. They are angry at the government and I am quite sure they are going to be angry at some of their own members-that is the Liberal members from the western provinces
for not standing up in this house and at least making an attempt to get a better deal for their people.
I was quite interested in some items that have appeared in the press, particularly one editorial that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press. Everybody knows that the Winnipeg Free Press has been a supporter of this government. It is known as a Liberal newspaper. This is what they have to say about the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker). This editorial is dated January 23, 1956 and reads as follows:
The constituency of Rosthern in Saskatchewan should consider itself well served. It has two House of Commons members. Official lists, it is true, show only Mr. Walter Tucker as the member. But lists are poor things. They cannot show that there is a western Mr. Tucker and there is also an eastern Mr. Tucker, quite distinct.

On the afternoon of October 17 the executive of the Liberal association met, 50 strong, in Rosthern. That evening the western Mr. Tucker wired Prime Minister St. Laurent and Trade Minister Howe and, on behalf of the meeting, pressed for cash advances on farm stored grain.
But the air of Ottawa has caused a strange metamorphosis: and on January 17 the eastern Tucker rose in the House of Commons and repudiated the western Tucker. The eastern Tucker was not only against cash advances on farm stored grain. More than that: he charged that the C.C.F. party, by its advocacy of cash advances on such grains, was attempting to wreck the Canadian wheat board.
The implications of the eastern Tucker's charges are obvious; they charge the western Tucker with attempting to wreck the Canadian wheat board; for the western Tucker also advocated these cash advances.
The eastern Tucker was, of course, simply parroting Mr. Howe. But he seems to be stepping beyond the line of duty, or even the requirements of expediency, when he carries Mr. Howe's theory of guilt by association even farther than Mr. Howe did. It may be tempting to a Saskatchewan politician to feel that anything is good enough to throw at the C.C.F. But it is, apart from anything else, poor politics.
The charge that the C.C.F. is against the wheat board simply will not stick. And while Mr. Howe was wise enough to refrain from so direct an attack on the C.C.F., he was also kind enough to refrain from listing the Liberal Association of Rosthern, and the western Tucker as its spokesman, among the enemies of the wheat board. It really was rather cruel of the eastern Tucker to step in and do it himself.
That statement was printed prior to a report that was made by Mr. Arthur Blakely of the Montreal Gazette on January 20, with respect to a meeting that was held by the Liberal party the evening before. This report reads as follows:
The big Liberal party dinner honouring trade minister C. D. Howe and agriculture minister James G. Gardiner on the completion of 20 years of continuous service in the federal cabinet, turned out to be quite an affair. As a matter of fact, it still has the Liberal back benches buzzing.
I am going to leave out part of this statement and start in again where it is headed "Leadership Assured". Leadership was what they had been discussing.
The matter of leadership out of the way, the two honoured right honourables selected another text. At all costs, they advised Liberal backbenchers, toe the party line.
Mr. Howe was emphatic on this point. Ruggedly individualistic courses of action, by individual Liberals, could bring on trouble. And plenty of it. And in that way the existing Liberal majority- however large it might appear-could be wiped out.
Superb leadership had long been a Liberal asset. And when the Prime Minister had decided on a given course of action, that should be accepted as the proper policy by all true Liberals, whether they agreed with it or not. Decisions by the leadership were taken only with the greatest of care. And they could be disregarded only at the cost of inviting political disaster.
"We must pay a good deal of attention to the party line," Mr. Howe warned. "If the party is wrong, you are going to be defeated anyway. We stand or fall together."

Once this party line was laid down "I don't care whether you are a member of the House of Commons or the Senate, that line should be adhered to."
Later, in another section headed "Party Loyalty", we find this:
Mr. Gardiner, who has had his wayward moments on such issues as the $65 million payment to the wheat farmers and the south Saskatchewan dam project, added his plea.
"When the majority of the Liberal party agrees that a thing should be done, I'm going to work to see that it is done."
And he submitted, for consideration of the faithful, something in the way of an object lesson.
Years ago, when Mackenzie King had been prime minister the government accepted a decision which he had strongly opposed. In the commons, when the matter came under debate, Mr. King asked him to speak in support of the measure.
He did so. And with such effect that as he was leaving the house, a colleague stopped him offered his congratulations and said with admiration, what would you have sounded like had you really believed in what you were saying?
I take it from that, Mr. Speaker, that whenever the Minister of Agriculture speaks now we will not know whether or not he believes in what he is saying.
Last fall I attended a meeting of farmers. At the end of the meeting a farmer asked me this question. Is it true that there is a great deal of empty elevator space in the city of Saskatoon? He said he was talking to a man who worked there and he told him there was a lot of space in the elevator. My answer was that I could not conceive that there would be any elevator space in any terminal elevator in Canada at this time, because I thought the Minister of Trade and Commerce was too good a businessman to allow space to be empty when it was needed so badly, and when the farmers needed the money so badly.
I did not think very much more about my answer to that question until some time in November, when I picked up a copy of the Edmonton Journal in which there was a report of a meeting attended by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the city of Edmonton. I do not remember the exact figures, but the report was to the effect that there was a considerable amount of storage space available both at Vancouver and at the lakehead. On January 20, 1956, I asked this question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as reported at page 347 of Hansard:
Would the minister present the latest figures concerning the amount of empty space now available in terminal elevators?
I might say that the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) had stated in the course of his address that there was space available in the elevators for something
The Address-Mr. Campbell like 100 million bushels. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) interjected at that time and said, "No, the amount would not be much over half of that". When I got the answer to the question I found that the interior elevators had space available for 700,000 bushels of wheat; the Pacific coast terminals at Vancouver and New Westminster had space for
8.200.000	bushels; Victoria, 400,000 bushels; Prince Rupert 700,000 bushels; and Churchill
600.000	bushels.
I am not going to say anything about the eastern terminals because the minister pointed out that as the lakes were frozen we could expect to have quite a lot of space available there. I find, however, that the space available in western elevators amounted to
44.700.000	bushels. Well, there is something wrong there. There must be a nigger in the woodpile somewhere. Who is responsible?
I have always believed that the responsibility lay with the transport controller. In the debate a few days ago we were given to understand that the railroads were making the adjustments and saying where the railroad cars were going to go. This is a serious situation.
I shall refer to only the effective amount of storage, because as the minister said the other day they want to keep 10 per cent of the space available in case a certain amount of the grain has to be dried or something like that. The effective storage space available now is 44,700,000 bushels. One of the suggestions I am going to make is this. We should get the transport controller to work. We should make that name plate on his door worth something. We should see that cars are made available so this space in the terminal elevators could be filled. I believe the transport controller should be given orders to get this done and get it done quickly. If it were done, and done rapidly, we could then distribute to the farmers $53,640,000- without any cost to the government and without making any loans. I am going to prophesy right here that this is a far greater amount of money than will be borrowed by the farmers under the loan scheme.
I want an answer to these questions, and I hope some minister will give that answer. The Minister of Agriculture has not spoken as yet. I am sure the farmers of this country and the members of this parliament will want to know why this space has not been filled. Have the railroads been going on their own without any direction? Is it because the Crowsnest rates are low? Speaking in Montreal a few days ago the presidents of both railways objected to the Crowsnest pass rates. They claimed that those rates were only one-third of the rates they were getting
506	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Campbell on some other products. Are the railways passing up the hauling of wheat because they can make more money on other products? If that is the case it is time the controller stepped in and saw to it that the farmers in western Canada got their fair share of box cars.
Are we short of box cars? The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce said some new box cars were going to be made available soon. We have had this trouble in other years, and the transport controller was appointed to do just what he should have been doing during these past months. We had trouble when the lake boats were hauling iron ore and passing up the hauling of wheat. If the government sees to it that the transport controller goes to work and makes cars available to fill this space, then this $50 or $60 million can be paid to the farmers as soon as that grain is delivered. It is a pity it could not have been done before, because the farmers in western Canada are running up against another problem, something that is new.
Our crises follow each other in succession year after year. We have never experienced this crisis before, though I remember one winter in 1906-07 when we had a tremendous amount of snow. Today the roads in western Canada are blocked with snow. There is so much snow it is almost impossible to clear it. I have been getting letters and I have been reading in the papers about farmers trying to get into town by means of teams of horses. They have not many horses, and the horses they have cannot work because they have not done any work for two or three years. It is going to be almost impossible for many farmers to deliver much grain, even if box cars are made available, unless the government accepts the suggestion I am now going to make.
About the only farmers who are going to be able to deliver grain are those living on built-up highways which are snowplowed. The back concession roads cannot be opened and probably will not be opened until May. I suggest that the farmers who live in the back concessions be allowed to exchange wheat with the farmers who live on the built-up roads, so the farmers in the back concessions can get some money out of the little quota that is to be made available, I do not know when.
My other suggestion is this. To put a little more money in the pockets of the farmers, enough to keep them going, the government should make an interim payment on the 1954-55 crop, and make it soon. These are my suggestions.


I now wish to say something about the wheat surplus. Since a lot has been said about this surplus I am not going to repeat what has been said up to now, but my attention has been drawn to an editorial that appeared in the Western Producer of December 1, 1955. It is a long editorial, and of course I cannot put it all on Hansard. It deals with FAO and what FAO was set up for. The Minister of Agriculture should tell this house why FAO has failed and why something has not been done along the lines of the great plans that the people who set up FAO had for the handling of surpluses.
As I said, I am not going to read the whole editorial because it is too long, but I am going to read a short extract from what President Eisenhower had to say about surpluses a year after he took office. The editorial reads:
Here is President Eisenhower speaking after a year in office and declaring a new kind of total war:
"... total war, not upon any human enemy, but upon the brute forces of poverty and need. The peace we seek, founded upon decent trust and co-operative effort amongst nations, can be fortified-not by weapons of war, but by wheat and cotton, by milk and wool, by meat, by timber and by rice. These are words that translate into every language of the globe."
What an exhilarating prospect but what a bleak realization with Mr. Benson today wringing his hands over unsaleable surpluses and calling for sharp cuts in production!
More recently there was Sir Anthony Eden to this effect:
"We all know what unparalleled resources the scientific and technical advances of the age have placed within our reach. We have only to stretch out our hand and the human race can enter an era of prosperity, such as has never been seen."
The other day the foreign office called Bulganin hypocritical. What would be the appropriate term for Sir Anthony who dares talk about "only stretching out the hand" well aware that "the hungry sheep look up and are not fed."
One could quote interminably in this vein from the great and near-great of the world, but we must content ourselves with only another from Lord Boyd-Orr, first FAO chairman. A few months ago he complained of international conferences "talking about isms instead of about food and food production where they would know what they were talking about." In the same speech he said:
"In a world where two-thirds of the people are hungry, there is no world food surplus. If the plans which FAO put forward in 1946 had been carried through, there would have been a big world reserve of food, with a big fund behind it, and in the countries where there was a surplus, that would have been bought and the farmers would have got the money and the food would have been sold to the countries that were hungry."
I come to another matter I wish to discuss, namely air mail service to the town of Lloyd-minster in Saskatchewan. When the former minister of finance, Mr. Abbott, introduced

this legislation he made a definite commitment to this house. He was talking about the increase in the postal rates on first-class mail. He said:
When the new rates come into effect all first-class mail will be carried by air it air carriage will speed up delivery. Canada already has the most advanced air mail service of any country in the world and this service will be further improved.
This quotation may be found in Hansard of Tuesday, December 8, 1953, at page 691.
The chamber of commerce of the town of Lloydminster, the board of trade of North Battleford, and the provincial board of trade have all passed resolutions and have all written the government and the Post Office Department asking that this mail service be made available to the people in that community. The town of Lloydminster is situated on the border between the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. It was first settled by the Barr colony. It is also the centre of the first oil development in Saskatchewan.
I have not time to go into all the resolutions that were passed by these different organizations. I ask the government and the Postmaster General to see to it that the commitment that was made by Mr. Abbott when he was minister of finance is carried out, and that the benefits which can be derived by the carriage of mail by air be extended to that district.
There is another matter I might have brought up when I was discussing the wheat problem, namely inland storage. The board of trade of North Battleford and many farmers' organizations in that area have been requesting the government for years to do something about an interior elevator at that point. They have sent in resolution after resolution. I saw the Minister of Trade and Commerce about this matter several years ago. We think the time has now come when the Minister of Trade and Commerce should take a different look at this situation. Because the city of North Battleford is centrally located, wheat can be shipped to the port of Churchill in Hudson bay; it can be shipped to the west coast, or to the great lakes. I urge the Minister of Trade and Commerce to take another look at the suggestion and see if it would be possible to give us inland storage, which is needed so badly at that point.
I am going to make another suggestion to the Minister of Agriculture. I see he is just leaving the house. Perhaps he will sit down for a few minutes, because I will not take up very much more time.

We have heard a lot about diversification. At this time many of our
The Address-Mr. Batten farmers are wondering what would be the best course to take and where they can diversify their farm production. The Minister of Agriculture and his department should give more leadership than they are giving along those lines. I know of certain farmers who grew a considerable amount of rape last year. How many more acres of land can be put into rape? How many more cattle can be produced? How many hogs should we produce next year? How much land should be put down to grass, and so on and so forth?
I think the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and his department should give a lead. I heard Professor Ramsay speaking in Saskatoon a few days before I came here. He urged that the farmers go in for more cattle. He pointed out that in the past we had shipped more than 400,000 head of cattle to the United States in one year. The minister and his department are in a better position than anyone else to give leadership as to how much diversification there should be and what changes should be made. I would ask that he endeavour to do something between now and the spring, and that he give an indication to the farmers concerning the possibility of changing to other products, how much they might produce and how much they could expect to market in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I have the pleasure of joining with those who have preceded me in extending congratulations to the mover (Mrs. Shipley) and the seconder (Mr. Laflamme) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. May I also say I believe they have honourably discharged their responsibility, which in itself was an honour to them and to their constituencies.
Last session when I spoke in this debate I gave a description of the riding of Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, which is the riding I have the honour to represent. I do not propose to repeat that now, but there is one point I should like to mention. The industrial town of Corner Brook is situated at the mouth of the Humber river, at the bottom of Humber arm, 30 miles inland from the sea along the south shore of bay of Islands. In 1923 the settlement of Corner Brook consisted of just a few families who depended for their prosperity on the operation of a small lumbering industry. In that year the government of the day decided to build a paper mill on this site. Since that time it has grown to become the largest integrated pulp and paper mill in the world. It has a daily production of over 1,200 tons and at peak periods employs 10,000 peopje in the plant and the wood areas. Just to the east of Corner Brook is

The Address-Mr. Batten an area known as Corner Brook East, which is perhaps more familiarly known by Newfoundlanders as Humbermouth. This area for many years depended for its prosperity on the fact that it was a terminal for the Newfoundland railway. It still is a railway terminal for the C.N.R.
Just to the west of Corner Brook is an area known as Corner Brook West which grew up because of the operation of the paper mill there. Still further west is an area known as Curling, a very old and well established settlement. Heretofore these four townships were governed by separate town councils. Last spring a plebiscite was held and the people of the four areas voted to amalgamate and form one unit. In August of last year an election was held and a mayor and eight councillors were elected. On January 1 of this year, just about three weeks ago, these four townships were officially incorporated into the new city of Corner Brook, which is the second largest city in Newfoundland and the twenty-eighth in Canada.
The year 1955 was a prosperous year for Newfoundland. In fact I think I am able to say that it was the, most prosperous year in the entire history of Newfoundland. In those industries which brought prosperity to Newfoundland there was one exception, the fishing industry. The total landings of ground fish in 1955 amounted to 545 million pounds, with a value of $13-2 million. This was a. decrease of 62-4 million pounds or $1-5 million from the year 1954. The herring industry, which is particularly important in my area, also experienced a decrease in 1955. This decrease amounted to approximately 2 million pounds compared to the catch of 1954. On the other hand the lobster industry, which is also extremely important in my area, had an excellent year; 5-3 million pounds for the whole of Newfoundland were landed, with a value of $1-4 million. It is interesting to note here that since the year 1930 the lobster industry in Newfoundland has shown a continuous increase year after year. The year 1955 produced the highest catch of all the years since 1930. This increase has not been due solely to an increased number of fishermen engaged in that branch of the fishing industry, but is also due to the fact that regulations governing the lobster fishing industry were rigidly enforced, and it is also due to the co-operation of the fishermen themselves.
We all recognize that the provincial government in Newfoundland and the fishing industry itself are giving very serious consideration to what should be done to improve the status of those men who are engaged in that industry, but while I say that fishing 
is generally a provincial matter there is also a national aspect to that industry. In that respect I believe the federal government can do much to help in the work that is going on in Newfoundland to improve the lot of the fishermen, and I should like to make three suggestions.
I would suggest first-and this relates to my own riding in particular-that the federal Department of Fisheries make a complete survey of the fishing potential on the west coast of Newfoundland so the different types of fish, the quantity of fish and where the different types can be found will be known by those people who might be inclined to invest money in the fishing industry. In that way the government would be giving some guidance to those people who might invest money in the industry as is done, for example, for those who might invest money in mining.
Second, I would urge the Department of Fisheries to establish more bait depots along the coast, particularly in my own riding. We need bait depots for the operation of the industry. Some people ask why there is so much talk at this time about bait depots in Newfoundland when years ago the fishing industry was operating without the use of bait depots.
The answer, of course, is very simple. In the first place, in Newfoundland we do not now get the same adequate supplies of bait at the right time of year and in the right place that we used to get years ago. Second, if we are going to improve the lot of the fishermen it is necessary that they go to work earlier in the year and that they remain at their task until later in the year. In Newfoundland we are not able to secure sufficient fresh bait early in the year, nor are we able to secure sufficient fresh bait later on in the year to keep our men working long enough to increase their production sufficiently to give them a good return for their work. In the lobster industry in particular if fresh bait is not available at the time the lobster fishing begins, then the lobster fishermen are seriously handicapped.
The establishment of bait depots would be of vast assistance to them. In my area there is but one bait depot, at Port aux Choix, which was built three or four years ago. If the federal Department of Fisheries intended this to be an experiment I can assure the department that it has been highly successful; and in the light of what has been done in that area and from my own experience I know that the catch in that area has been more than doubled because of that bait depot. I suggest that bait depots be built at strategic points along this coast, and I would suggest

such points as Lark Harbour, Bonne Bay, Cow Head and Reefs Harbour.
My third suggestion does not apply to my own riding or province alone but to all parts of Canada where the fishing industry is prosecuted. I refer to unemployment insurance for fishermen. I believe that if unemployment insurance were extended to the fishermen of Canada it would do much to encourage them to carry on in the industry in which they make their living. Last year when the unemployment insurance commission presented its report to the committee we all noticed that it was a negative report. Maybe there were some who felt that a more positive approach would have been more acceptable, but on reflection I am not too sure that a negative approach is wrong. At least it does point out the obstacles which have to be overcome if we are to have fishermen included among those who are considered to be insurable.
These are the three suggestions I would make; first, a full-fledged survey of the fishing potential of the west coast of Newfoundland; second, the establishment of more bait depots, and third, the inclusion of fishermen in the unemployment insurance scheme.
I turn now to the problem of transportation in Newfoundland, and may I say that this has always been a big problem for us in the island province. For many years the only method of trans-insular transportation was by the Newfoundland railway. Although this railroad is of narrow gauge it has given real service to our island since the project was first discussed in 1847 and brought to practical reality by the railway bill of 1881. There has been a steady improvement in the services and facilities since the first crosscountry train left St. John's on July 24, 1898. We can trace its growth from the days when it was known as the Reid Newfoundland railway to the time it was operated as a state concern giving yeoman service during world war II, until finally it became a part of the Canadian National Railways in 1949.
Since confederation there has been a tremendous increase in the amount of traffic with which the Canadian National Railways in Newfoundland has had to cope. In 1955 carloadings were up 13 per cent over 1954. From 1949 to 1954 freight coming into Newfoundland from Nova Scotia was up 65 per cent; in the same period local freight was up 28 per cent; passenger traffic had increased by 17 per cent; express by 50 per cent, and the mail traffic had doubled.
A real effort has been made by the C.N.R. to cope with the problem of increasing traffic. The completion of the dieselization of the
The Address-Mr. Batten Newfoundland district, together with the increase in rolling stock, will do much to increase efficiency on the C.N.R. in Newfoundland. In addition I would suggest that the plans for the immediate future include the improvement of terminal facilities at Deer Lake, Corner Brook and the Stephenville area so as to provide a service more compatible with the growing needs of these expanding communities.
I recognize that a proportion of C.N.R. operations in Newfoundland have to do with the coastal steamship service. The problem here has been accentuated by a serious decrease in the number of vessels engaged in the local trade. If I may digress here for a moment I should like to support my colleague, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter), in the plea he made here the other evening for an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act so the annual inspection regulations which now apply to all vessels over 150 tons will apply only to vessels over 250 tons. Coming back again to the C.N.R., I believe that some of the problems with which they are now faced will be solved at least in part when the two new ships now under construction in the United Kingdom are put into service.
During the recess as I went around my riding I was happy to hear from time to time of the good work being done by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Health and Welfare. May I as a backbencher commend them for the stature which they have given to Canada in the councils of the world. They have discharged their responsibilities with credit to Canada and distinction to themselves.
I think it is true that we live in a world fraught with danger. I remember that a few years ago, before the atomic bomb became a reality, in certain circles there was some doubt as to what would happen if the atom were ever split. Some wondered if there would not be a chain reaction which would destroy the whole universe. Today we know that such a result is improbable, but I do not think that in the world in which we live today we are entirely out of the woods. The presence of the atomic and hydrogen bombs may, under certain conditions, initiate within the minds of men a chain reaction which may produce exactly the same effect.
I was pleased to note that in the speech from the throne mention was made of Canada's continued and further participation in the Colombo plan. In the awakening of nationalism in the countries of Asia there must of necessity be the growth of a desire
510	HOUSE OF
The Address-Miss Aitken on the part of the peoples concerned to improve their standards of living and take their places among the peoples of the world. The decision on the part of western countries to help them achieve that aim will have a real impact upon these countries, and we sincerely hope will be a stroke for the advancement of world peace.
During wartime the democratic nations of the world spent billions of dollars to ensure that man might swim through the sea like a fish. The democratic nations spent billions to ensure that man would fly through the air like a bird, and I think it is a great thing in peacetime that the free nations of the world can afford to spend a little in an attempt to ensure that free men will walk the earth as men.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to take part in the throne speech debate, but when I returned to Toronto this week end I received many messages, telephone calls and letters asking that I raise my voice in parliament on behalf of what could only be described as an aroused citizenry. The number of sex crimes which are taking place in and around Toronto and throughout the country have alarmed people right across the country. I know the Minister of Justice must feel sympathetic and appreciate the fear that parents have, and I know that all hon. members of this house must feel horror and revulsion on reading of these crimes which are increasing week by week.
Mr. Speaker, through you I do beseech the Minister of Justice to give leadership in this matter. As things stand now the people, and I am speaking particularly of Toronto, are far ahead of the government in their concern and fear, and in their determination that something must be done immediately. On Monday afternoon in Toronto a 13-year old girl, the victim of a sex maniac, was buried. A little more than a week ago in London a five-year old child, the victim of a sex maniac, was buried. In Hamilton eight women have been assaulted in as many weeks. After each of these crimes we read in the newspapers that the police have rounded up 300 or 400 known sex degenerates for questioning. Surely our laws are wrong, Mr. Speaker, when they allow 300 to 400 known suspects to roam the streets. Surely our laws are wrong when innocent little girls are the prey of these known maniacs.
We have been warned by medical men and psychiatrists that sex offenders are not responsible. You punish them but they strike again and again. Our magistrates and our judges are not doctors or psychiatrists, and in


our courts minor offenders of this nature are not recognized when they first appear in court. The result is that such afflicted people are not sent for the necessary treatment at a time when future crimes might be prevented. The permanent solution of this problem, it seems to me, rests with the government and the government alone. There must be a revision of our Criminal Code to provide for the holding of offenders or even suspects indefinitely, whether they be held in prison for crimes they have committed or whether they be held for psychiatric treatment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
In St. Catharines the other day a man committed an offence against two little girls and was taken to court. He pleaded guilty, but he claimed that he was drunk when he committed the offence. Press reports said that he was extremely embarrassed and contrite, but to be embarrassed and contrite was no comfort to the parents of those little girls or to the little girls themselves. However, it seemed to be some comfort to the judge, because he gave the man a suspended sentence of two years. If the man had stolen a motor rug from a parked car he would have received a greater sentence. I claim that the magistrate in giving that sentence was simply adding another young man to the 300 or 400 known persons suspected of sex deviation; yet the man's only defence was that he was drunk at the time.
Is it any wonder that citizens are aroused? Under the Criminal Code the maximum penalty for rape is life imprisonment. Yet last September here in Ottawa a man who had committed rape was given 10 years. Under our Criminal Code indecent assault calls for a

maximum penalty of five years. Yet in Toronto within the past few months a youth of 19 assaulted a nine-year-old girl and was given nine months.
I know that a royal commission under Chief Justice McRuer is engaged at the present time in studying aspects of this terrible problem and, as I understand it, the report is to be forthcoming within the next few months. But, Mr. Speaker-and again I am speaking not only for my own constituents but for many thousands of parents in Toronto-we cannot wait for that academic and careful study while these murders are taking place.
In Toronto an organization was formed some time ago called the parents' action league. Its purpose is not to study the problem but to take action, to go on the offensive against this scourge of our society. Like all modern societies it is becoming known by its initials and is referred to as PAL. The parents' action league is urging that magistrates send sex offenders or even suspects to hospitals for psychiatric study. The provincial government of Ontario is trying to co-operate within the confines of its authority. Offenders are to be segregated at Guelph reformatory and an extension of psychiatric facilities is to be carried out in all Ontario hospitals.
The parents' action league now represents about 70 organizations. Indeed, I think you can say it represents three million people in the province of Ontario. But it is not the parents' action league or any other citizens' group that can give leadership in solving this problem. We the people are calling on the Minister of Justice, who tells us that the code is there, to take action. It is the setting up of psychiatric institutions that is needed. It is a cure, a preventative that is needed, and I feel that is the responsibility of the dominion government.
Even before the royal commission finishes its deliberations it is essential to take known sex degenerates out of circulation. At the funeral of little five-year-old Susan Cadieux of London, who was assaulted and murdered, Father O'Rourke had this to say:
Degenerates like mad dogs are allowed to roam our streets at will.
In the press report of that tragic funeral there was one sentence that caught my eye, and it was this:
In that assemblage of people the shame and degradation of one man rests on all men.
Through you, Mr. Speaker, I do beseech the Minister of Justice to give us the leadership in solving this problem for which people are asking. Throughout our society fear and horror run rampant while we wait for the government to assume its responsibility and take action.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to extend the traditional congratulations to the mover (Mrs. Shipley) and seconder (Mr. Laflamme) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and more particularly to the hon. member for Timiskaming because she is something in the nature of a trail blazer and very possibly the honour accorded to her now may be the augury of greater things to come in the legislative councils of the country.
In this debate many hon. members have complained of the paucity of information contained in the speech from the throne and the legislative program of the government. I think, however, this is probably understandable, because if the government does not intend to submit legislation to parliament but rather intends to deal with matters by the more expeditious method of order in council, why bother announcing legislation in the speech from the throne?
As usually happens in debates of this type, the more interesting points are often raised in speeches from the opposition side of the house. I was particularly interested in the speech of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, who chose to complain of the influx of United States capital in the development of the resources of this country. I do not happen to share his alarm in this respect, because I believe that capital is essential for the development of the country. If a foreign nation chooses to put its capital into our country, I believe we should welcome it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Saskatchewan goes begging for it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I also note that in a recent address Mr. Muir, the president of the Royal Bank of Canada, stated that while in the occasional field this type of investment was excessive, on the whole he did not think it was nearly as bad as many people thought it was. I therefore do not think it is a subject that should give us too much concern. As a matter of fact we ought to welcome it, because we want to see our resources developed and we want to see our country grow. It certainly cannot grow without financial resources.
I also noted that the hon. member for Yorkton was greatly concerned about three large soap companies and bemoaned the fact that Canadians were unable to participate in these organizations. For his information I may say that all three companies have their securities listed on the New York stock exchange, and they are available to him by the simple expedient of going down to his bank and placing an order. He can become a partner in any of these organizations and

The Address-Mr. Trainor can participate in the enormous profits that he appears to think are available there.
All this stuff is typical of the sniping at private business that is indulged in by the socialists and, I may say, by the Liberal socialists of whom there appear to be more than a few in the present government. This is merely a manifestation of the operation of the free market. There is no greater guarantee of freedom, economic and political, than that which exists through the operation of the free market. When a man buys something on the free market he is, in effect, casting his vote as a citizen in a free economy. True, his vote may be outweighted by other votes, but the sum total of those votes will determine the economic outlook of the people. There does not seem to be any possibility of achieving such economic freedom under any other system. I know that the socialists argue in favour of what I think they call the controlled economy. Is that the expression they use?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The monopolistic system is what we have.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You would substitute the controlled economy. Is not that the expression you use?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Control by the many instead of by the few.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
All right. Let us take the controlled economy as an example. How would it work? I submit that it would be impossible to have political freedom under such a system because such a system would mean that the government would operate all business enterprises and all features of the economy. How would it be possible to hold democratic elections under such a system? I think it would be impossible to hold democratic elections. One would be obliged to resort to elections in the Russian style, with one party and one slate of candidates.
It is no accident that the Russians resort to this system. It is simply the result of a controlled economy. You might just as well explode a bomb under the economy as hold an election under those circumstances. You cannot take the directing heads of a business out of their chairs whenever you feel like it without producing a drastic effect on the operation of the business. The holding of an election would simply be taking the directors out of their directing chairs. The socialists and the Liberal socialists are merely trying to bribe the citizens of the country to relinquish their freedom as the price of so-called security. In other words the choice is between liberty and a mess of security pottage.
As a member representing a western constituency I would feel somewhat remiss in


my duty if I omitted all reference to wheat. It is not that I know much about wheat, but I hear a good deal about it and about its effect on the economy of western Canada. To my mind there are two separate and distinct problems involved in the wheat situation. The one is immediate. It is the problem of relieving the crisis that exists in the western economy. Judging from the debates here there seems to be only one logical way of achieving this end, namely by putting money in the pockets of the farmers, which money in turn will permeate the whole economy. It seems that the simplest and easiest way of achieving this end is to grant advances on farm-stored grain. The government have introduced substitute measures providing loans at 5 per cent and the payment of storage charges. These provisions seem to be inadequate; at least they are so interpreted by the farmers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I thought the hon. member was in favour of private industry?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: This is an emergency problem.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You want the government to get into this.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
This is a fire, a conflagration that is burning in the economy. You must do something about it. I say it is an immediate problem. I do not suggest that procedure as a permanent practice because I do not believe that even the western farmer would wish to the supported in perpetuity on the charity of the Canadian taxpayer. A different solution must be found for the long-term problem, but the immediate problem must be met in this way because the situation has gone too far. It is the moral responsibility of this government to do it.
After all, they said in effect to the western farmer, "We will buy your wheat and we will dispose of it. It is definitely illegal for you to dispose of it in any way except through us." If there is not a moral obligation implicit in that statement, I do not know what a moral obligation is. Therefore I say that the immediate obligation is the payment of advances on farm-stored grain. If there is any member from a western rural riding, a grain-growing riding, who wishes to dispute that I would challenge him to appear on the public platform in his constituency and say that he did not believe advances on farm-stored grain was the correct solution, but that the government plan of 5 per cent loans was right. He should take heed, however, of the experience of the Minister of Justice in this regard. He tried it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I tried it in my constituency in two or three places.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not know what your experience was, but I do know what the experience of the Minister of Justice was. The press reports state that his suggestion was greeted by hoots of derision. If other members chose to do that they would probably receive a similar response.
However, that is only the immediate question. There is the whole question of agricultural marketing which seems to bedevil this country, and has done so for some years. So far as we can see it is probably going to continue to do so. There has to be some constructive solution found for this difficulty. I would make a simple suggestion to the Prime Minister. We have heard a good deal of special pleading and a number of exparte solutions presented here. One does not always like to depend upon amateurs for a solution to this type of problem. I believe this problem demands the best brains we have in the country; therefore I suggest that the Prime Minister set up a royal commission to solve the marketing problems of this country, not only with regard to wheat but for agricultural products as a whole. Possibly such a commission might come forward with a solution. If not, they would at least have amassed all the evidence and there would be a basis for an intelligent discussion of the subject. I offer this solution very humbly as something of which the Prime Minister might take note.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to call attention to what I think is an extraordinary departure in the field of diplomatic procedure. I refer to a current periodical, to wit Look, in which appears an article by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) presuming to lecture the United States administration about the deficiencies of their foreign policy. I am not prepared to criticize the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Perhaps this is the new diplomacy. If so, I would suggest that he let us have a very good look at it, because to my mind it has implications that go far beyond the simple presentation of a point of view. This procedure would probably be all right if you could hold it to a one-way street, but you cannot very well indulge in such opinion presentation without conceding the other fellow the right to do likewise.
We may have an exchange of diplomatic opinion carried out through the periodical press. I would hesitate to peruse our periodical press if I were to find that Mr. Dulles had been belabouring the conduct of foreign affairs in this country. I do not feel it would be quite proper; it would be an offence against propriety. As a matter of fact this practice is rather insidious, because we do not know where it might end. It could even end up 67509-33
The Address*-Mr. Masse that we might have interference in domestic fields as well as foreign affairs. We might have the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, or even the Prime Minister appearing on the hustings in the United States in defence of the Democratic party. I have no doubt they would be very welcome.
On the other hand, we would have to expect the reverse of that. We might be faced with having Dean Acheson, Mr. Truman and others of the Democratic party up here trying to hold the fort for the weakening Liberal party.

It may be that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has discovered a new modus operandi, shall we say? Perhaps the whole pattern of diplomatic exchange is going to change. However, I can see implications that are not altogether palatable, and I do not believe they would be palatable to many in the country.

The subject matter of my speech will therefore be as follows: the past, the present and the constituency of Kamouraska, for which I have great admiration, like Mr. Arthur Buies, who wrote such interesting chronicles about that community.
Each session, since I have the privilege of sitting in this house, I have heard nothing

The Address-Mr. Masse but complaints and lamentations from my hon. friends opposite. Yet, we have had a by-election in Quebec, in a riding quite close to mine, and the people of Temiscouata, who are close friends of the citizens of the constituency of Kamouraska, did not hesitate to renew their confidence in the Liberal party.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They have felt quite disappointed since.

speechtext:
If the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne) spoke at the time as he did in the house this afternoon, I am not at all surprised with the result.
I went into that constituency not to make promises but to tell the people I am convinced that the Liberal party was doing its best to maintain unity in this country and to ensure the proper balance of our national economy.
As a son of a farming family, whose members have been living for generations on the family farm, I like to keep myself abreast of the development of my district, while at the same time keeping informed about what is happening outside.
In order to answer the arguments of those who claim that everything is amiss in this country, I should like to quote an article from the publication "1955 Report on the Prairie Provinces". I will not quote the whole article; it would be somewhat too long and especially too disastrous for our hon. friends opposite.
(Text) :
An agricultural province must take a longterm view of things. With this in mind, it is revealing that Saskatchewan farms have a record of production, particularly during the past ten years, that has no equal for an area of similar size and population.
The extent of the Saskatchewan market can be appreciated when we consider that from 1944 to 1954, inclusive, 112,000 farmers in this province produced wheat, coarse grains, livestock, poultry and eggs, dairy and miscellaneous products to a value exceeding $6 billion.
Manufacturing in Saskatchewan has also been on the ascent, with the result that during the same period our factories have produced goods to the value of over $2 billion.
(Translation):
The article continues in about the same vein.
(Text):
Industrial development in this province continues to show encouraging growth. During 1954, 341 new companies were incorporated, with a total capital of over $47 million.
(Translation):
And now I should like to quote an article from the Monetary Times concerning the province of Quebec:

(Text):
The year 1955 surprised economists. After a slow start, the pace of production seemed to quicken. Experts hope that when all the statistics are assembled, the present year will prove to have been the most prosperous in the history of the province.
The people of Quebec have never forgotten the heroic efforts of their ancestors to clear, possess and maintain the land they own, the success of today and the hope of the future.
Agricultural production is down slightly this year. Preliminary estimates suggest net value of farm output was $325-2 millions, compared with $325-9 millions in 1954.
Farm cash income dropped somewhat this year. (Translation):
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that prices of agricultural products have decreased to a certain extent in the course of the year. We cannot deny statistics. However, in the light of the extracts I quoted from the Monetary Times, it seems to me that we should be happy with the progress made by Canada during the last year.
Like the hon. members who preceded me, I have listened to and reread the speech from the throne, and I am still convinced it has been conceived with the purpose of serving the interests of the whole of Canada. Of course, the leaders of our country are men and, admittedly, anything human must fall short of perfection. Nevertheless, I remain convinced that the Liberal party does its best to maintain unity between the various groups making up the Canadian nation. With the best of goodwill, it cannot perform miracles. It cannot change wheat into uranium, nor surpluses into dollar bills. However, it must be admitted that the speech from the throne is so conceived as to balance the economy of the country.
